984: // start runs one clabwire capture and reports its packets, audit records and end as events.
985: func (c *captureChain) start(ctx context.Context, duration time.Duration) *captureSegment {
986: 	segmentCtx, cancel := context.WithCancel(ctx)
987: 	stdinReader, stdinWriter := io.Pipe()
988: 	segment := &captureSegment{
989: 		index: c.segments, localStart: time.Now(), duration: duration, cancel: cancel,
990: 		closeStdin: func() { _ = stdinWriter.Close() },
991: 	}
992: 	c.segments++
993: 
994: 	command := []string{
995: 		clabwireManager, "node-runtime", "packet-capture",
996: 		"--nodeName", c.group.location.NodeName,
997: 		"--format", "pcapng",
998: 		"--snapLength", strconv.Itoa(c.capture.req.SnapLength),
999: 		"--duration", duration.String(),
1000: 		clabwireStopOnStdinClose,
1001: 	}
1002: 	for _, name := range c.group.interfaces {
1003: 		command = append(command, "--interface", name)
1004: 	}
1005: 	if c.capture.req.PacketLimit > 0 {
1006: 		remaining := int64(c.capture.req.PacketLimit) - c.capture.out.Written()
1007: 		command = append(command, "--packetLimit",
1008: 			strconv.FormatInt(min(max(remaining, 1), maxClabwirePackets), 10))
1009: 	}
1010: 
1011: 	send := func(event segmentEvent) {
1012: 		event.segment = segment
1013: 		select {
1014: 		case c.events <- event:
1015: 		case <-segmentCtx.Done():
1016: 		}
1017: 	}
1018: 
1019: 	stdoutReader, stdoutWriter := io.Pipe()
1020: 	stderr := &auditLineWriter{send: func(audit *captureAudit) { send(segmentEvent{audit: audit}) }}
1021: 
1022: 	// The exec outlives the segment's context by up to captureStdinCloseGrace: when the segment
1023: 	// ends for any reason (the capture is cancelled or failed, the output failed, or a newer
1024: 	// segment took over), its stdin is closed first so clabwire ends on its own, and the stream
1025: 	// is cut only if it does not.
1026: 	execCtx, cancelExec := context.WithCancel(context.WithoutCancel(segmentCtx))
1027: 	execDone := make(chan struct{})
1028: 
1029: 	c.wg.Add(3)
1030: 	readDone := make(chan error, 1)
1031: 	go func() {
1032: 		defer c.wg.Done()
1033: 		readDone <- c.readSegment(stdoutReader, func(packet *clabcapture.Packet) {
1034: 			send(segmentEvent{packet: packet})
1035: 		})
1036: 		_, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, stdoutReader)
1037: 	}()
1038: 	go func() {
1039: 		defer c.wg.Done()
1040: 		select {
1041: 		case <-execDone:
1042: 			return
1043: 		case <-segmentCtx.Done():
1044: 		}
1045: 		segment.closeStdin()
1046: 		grace := time.NewTimer(captureStdinCloseGrace)
1047: 		defer grace.Stop()
1048: 		select {
1049: 		case <-execDone:
1050: 		case <-grace.C:
1051: 			log.Debug("Capture segment did not end after its stdin closed, cutting the stream",
1052: 				"node", c.group.display, "segment", segment.index)
1053: 			cancelExec()
1054: 		}
1055: 	}()
1056: 	go func() {
1057: 		defer c.wg.Done()
1058: 		defer cancel()
1059: 		defer cancelExec()
1060: 
1061: 		err := c.capture.r.execInPodContainer()(execCtx, c.group.location.Namespace,
1062: 			c.group.location.Pod, clabwireContainer, command, stdinReader, stdoutWriter, stderr)
1063: 		close(execDone)
1064: 		// the process ended: release the stdin copy of the exec stream
1065: 		segment.closeStdin()
1066: 		_ = stdoutWriter.Close()
1067: 		readErr := <-readDone
1068: 		stderr.flush()
1069: 		if err == nil && readErr != nil {
1070: 			err = readErr
1071: 		}
1072: 		if err != nil && stderr.text() != "" {
1073: 			if unsupported := unsupportedClabwire(
1074: 				c.group.location,
1075: 				stderr.text(),
1076: 			); unsupported != nil {
1077: 				err = unsupported
1078: 			} else {
1079: 				err = fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", err, stderr.text())
1080: 			}
1081: 		}
1082: 		send(segmentEvent{done: true, err: err})
1083: 	}()
1084: 
1085: 	return segment
1086: }

1088: // unsupportedClabwire recognizes a clabwire that rejects --stop-on-stdin-close, which every
1089: // capture passes: its release predates the capture contract the runtime needs.
1090: func unsupportedClabwire(location clablabruntime.NodeLocation, stderr string) error {
1091: 	if !strings.Contains(stderr, "flag provided but not defined") ||
1092: 		!strings.Contains(stderr, strings.TrimPrefix(clabwireStopOnStdinClose, "-")) {
1093: 		return nil
1094: 	}
1095: 
1096: 	return &unsupportedClabernetesError{reason: fmt.Sprintf(
1097: 		"clabwire in pod %s/%s does not accept packet-capture %s",
1098: 		location.Namespace, location.Pod, clabwireStopOnStdinClose)}
1099: }

1101: // readSegment checks that a segment's interfaces are the requested ones and passes its packets
1102: // on with the segment's interface index.
1103: func (c *captureChain) readSegment(stdout io.Reader, packet func(*clabcapture.Packet)) error {
1104: 	reader := clabcapture.NewReader(stdout)
1105: 	interfaces := 0
1106: 	for {
1107: 		event, err := reader.Next()
1108: 		if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
1109: 			return nil
1110: 		}
1111: 		if errors.Is(err, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF) {
1112: 			// the process was stopped inside a block
1113: 			return nil
1114: 		}
1115: 		if err != nil {
1116: 			return fmt.Errorf("failed to read the clabwire capture: %w", err)
1117: 		}
1118: 		if event.Interface != nil {
1119: 			if interfaces >= len(c.group.interfaces) ||
1120: 				event.Interface.Name != c.group.interfaces[interfaces] {
1121: 				return fmt.Errorf("clabwire described interface %q, want %s in order",
1122: 					event.Interface.Name, strings.Join(c.group.interfaces, ", "))
1123: 			}
1124: 			interfaces++
1125: 			continue
1126: 		}
1127: 		if event.Packet != nil {
1128: 			packet(event.Packet)
1129: 		}
1130: 	}
1131: }

1133: // auditLineWriter parses clabwire's stderr: audit records go to send, other lines are kept for
1134: // error messages.
1135: type auditLineWriter struct {
1136: 	send func(*captureAudit)
1137: 
1138: 	mu      sync.Mutex
1139: 	partial []byte
1140: 	other   []string
1141: }
1142: 
1143: func (w *auditLineWriter) Write(data []byte) (int, error) {
1144: 	w.mu.Lock()
1145: 	w.partial = append(w.partial, data...)
1146: 	var lines [][]byte
1147: 	for {
1148: 		idx := bytes.IndexByte(w.partial, '\n')
1149: 		if idx < 0 {
1150: 			break
1151: 		}
1152: 		lines = append(lines, append([]byte(nil), w.partial[:idx]...))
1153: 		w.partial = w.partial[idx+1:]
1154: 	}
1155: 	w.mu.Unlock()
1156: 
1157: 	for _, line := range lines {
1158: 		w.line(line)
1159: 	}
1160: 
1161: 	return len(data), nil
1162: }
1163: 
1164: func (w *auditLineWriter) flush() {
1165: 	w.mu.Lock()
1166: 	line := w.partial
1167: 	w.partial = nil
1168: 	w.mu.Unlock()
1169: 	if len(bytes.TrimSpace(line)) != 0 {
1170: 		w.line(line)
1171: 	}
1172: }
1173:

2. Race: `handle` runs on the chain's single goroutine (events channel), so segment field access is single-threaded, except `stopTimer` AfterFunc callback `active.closeStdin` — closes stdin writer, safe (io.Pipe Close is safe).

3. `setCut` computes stopTimer duration: `c.cut - c.next.started.UnixNano() + window`. cut = overlapStart + overlap/2 where overlapEnd = active.plannedEnd. cut - nextStarted = overlap/2. So AfterFunc fires at overlap/2 + window after next Started. OK.

4. Potential deadlock: `c.events` is buffered 256. `send` blocks if channel full and segmentCtx not done. The chain loop reads events. When chain is in `drain()`, it consumes events. When chain returns (e.g., error), `defer` runs drain, which consumes events until wg done. The segment goroutines: the stdout reader goroutine sends packets; after chain returned with error, drain consumes them. wg includes 3 goroutines per segment. readSegment goroutine ends after readDone sent and io.Copy finishes... Actually the reader goroutine sends `readDone <- err` first (buffered 1), then io.Copy(io.Discard, stdoutReader) until stdoutReader EOF — stdoutWriter closed by exec goroutine after exec returns. Then wg.Done. The exec goroutine waits `readErr := <-readDone` — readDone has buffer 1, so ok.

But one subtle deadlock: the exec goroutine writes packets to `stdoutWriter` (io.Pipe). If the chain has returned and drain is consuming events, ok. But if the segment's stdout reader is blocked in `send` while the chain goroutine is blocked... chain always consumes. OK.

If one chain errors, others keep streaming until... the erroring chain returned but other chains are not cancelled! `groupCtx` is only cancelled when all return or Wait returns? errgroup: Wait returns after all goroutines return; ctx is cancelled when the first function returns non-nil error. Actually, wait — potential unbounded memory: while stopping, the chain keeps receiving packet events from segments and appends next's packets to held; the emit path... parts.text:
One observation: when `FinishOnCancel` is set and the capture finishes cleanly (e.g., duration expires) before the user presses Ctrl+C again, the process exits normally — but the signal-handler goroutine remains blocked on `<-sigs`, which is fine.

However, there's a subtle issue: the second signal during "stopping" exits with code 1 — reasonable.

Another consideration: `defer o.Global.FinishOnCancel.Store(false)` in captureFn — if captureFn returns normally and the user had already sent one Ctrl+C... The context cancel triggers capture end; captureFn returns nil; the goroutine is still waiting for the second signal. Then main returns and the process exits. Fine.

But there's a subtle race: after `FinishOnCancel.Store(false)` (defer runs at captureFn exit), if the handler goroutine is between `GetOptions()` and the `Load()`... Actually the handler reads options once via GetOptions at that point; the `Load()` happens right after. Sequence: signal arrives → cancel() → GetOptions() → Load(). If the capture ends before the signal arrives, no issue. If the signal arrives just before captureFn's defer resets the flag, the handler sees true and waits for a second signal — process exits normally when main returns. No leak issue beyond a goroutine.

parts.text:
I've now seen the core of the c9s capture.go. Let me look at the remaining diff regions I haven't seen closely: the docs (docs/cmd/capture.md, docs/manual/clabernetes/runtime.md, docs/manual/wireshark.md, docs/cmd/inspect/interfaces.md), and the test files (capture/local_test.go, pcapng_test.go, reorder_test.go, cmd/capture_test.go, core/capture_test.go, labruntime_cluster_test.go, clabernetes/capture_test.go), plus `.github/workflows` changes already seen, and the diff for `core/test_data/capture.clab.yml` (seen at 3490-3510).

Also need to check `cmd/capture.go`'s `-w -` stdout behavior vs. logs; and check the schema — `clab.schema.json` relates to topology files; new test topo uses standard fields (links type host, host-interface). No new topology keys, so no schema change needed.

Now let me focus on hunting for real defects. Key areas to check:

1. **`Output.Emit` packet limit counting vs. written**: limit counts handed-to-stream, fine.

2. **Reorder `Push` when `q.err != nil`**: returns q.err. OK.

3. **Reorder.Run timer busy-loop**: `wait = max(next.Sub(q.now()), time.Millisecond)` — if due already passed (negative), 1ms → loops at 1ms until due processed. Fine.

4. **`writeDue` holds scan**: iterates `q.holds` map each call — fine, few holds.

5. **`Reorder.Push` cursor check**: `q.cursor != 0 && packet.Timestamp < q.cursor`. Cursor is the max timestamp written in order. But early `writeLocked` in Push (late packet) writes without advancing cursor. However, the late packet may have a timestamp greater than cursor but... no, it's less. Fine.

But subtle: cursor is updated by popLocked via `max(q.cursor, item.packet.Timestamp)`. Once a packet was written out of order (late) with a timestamp *greater* than cursor... can that happen? A late packet has Timestamp < cursor, so no.

But wait: what about a packet written directly when window <= 0 — cursor never advances, irrelevant.

Another subtle issue: after a late packet is written out of order, subsequent packets with timestamps between the late packet's and cursor are also "late" — correct behavior.

6. **`Output.Close`**: cancelRun, wait runDone, Flush. But `Emit` may still be called concurrently after Close? CaptureLocal: readers exit before out.Close is called (wg.Wait). c9s: group.Wait then out.Close. OK.

7. **Potential goroutine leak in `Output`**: runDone closed on cancelRun; reorder.Run returns on ctx done. OK.

8. **`Reorder.Push` after `Flush`**: In c9s Capture, after out.Close()... chains already done. OK.

9. **`capture/local.go` `drain`** — `r.out.Emit` may return error → return. Also `time.Now().Before(deadline)` where deadline = end+250ms. But `drain` is called with `time.Now()` at ctx done. OK.

10. **`localReader.run` ctx check**: after `stop()` (packet limit reached), Emit returns false → return without drain. Fine.

11. **CaptureLocal openAll**: if `l.open` returns fewer/more sources... only with test stubs. Fine.

12. **`openPacketSockets`**: on error closes only sources opened so far in this namespace — but sources from previous nodes were appended; closeAll closes all non-nil. Good.

13. **afpacket**: `OptFrameSize(blockSize)` — TPacket frame size must be >= block size? In gopacket afpacket, for TPACKET_V3, frame size and block size are set; block size must be multiple of frame size and page size... Setting both equal to blockSize (1MiB) with 8 blocks = 8MiB ring per interface. Fine.

14. **pcapng `Writer.WritePacket`**: body cap `20+len+3` — padding at most 3. Good.

15. **`Reader.Next` peek at SHB**: If SHB is the last block and stream ends right after 8-byte header, Peek(4) returns ErrUnexpectedEOF — but the stream might legitimately end... a truncated stream. Acceptable.

16. **`pcapngNanosecondsFrom`**: tsresol raw value semantics: if_tsresol byte: most significant bit 0 → power of 10; value = exponent. So tsresol=9 → nanoseconds. `tsresol > pcapngNanoseconds` rejects e.g. 10..127, allows 0..9. And msb set → fractional (2^-n) — rejected. Comment says "Only decimal resolutions up to nanoseconds occur in clabwire streams." OK.

17. **`Reader` interface dedup between segments**: interfaces reset on new section. Packets reference ID per current section. OK.

18. **`Reorder` window vs c9s hold**: hold at cut-W; held packets of next with timestamps ≥ cut-W are emitted after active ends; the hold prevents other chains' packets with timestamps > cut-W from being written before the switch. Good.

19. **`switchSegments` gap reporting when `c.cut != 0`**: condition `if c.next == nil || c.next.started.IsZero() || c.cut == 0` → report gap. But when cut != 0 and next.started != 0, no gap — correct since overlap existed.

However — hmm, there's a subtle bug candidate: `c.cut == 0` also happens when `setCut` found the overlap too short (< 2*window). In that case the switch is reported as a gap — but packets from both segments in the overlap may double! If overlap < 2*window, the cut is not set, active streams until it ends (no dropping at cut), and held packets of next are all emitted (cut==0 → no dedup) → **duplicate packets in the overlap**. The comment in setCut says "the switch is reported as a gap" — but the overlap packets would be duplicated, not missing. Actually wait: when overlap is too short, the gap is reported (From active end / plannedEnd, To next.started). But the next segment started before active ended — packets captured by both during the overlap are emitted twice (active emits until it ends; then held of next all emitted with cut==0). Hmm, but actually does the overlap < 2*window case happen in practice? overlap = min(maxCaptureOverlap, segment/3). window = min(maxCaptureCutWindow, overlap/4). So window = overlap/4 when overlap < 2000ms → 2*window = overlap/2 < overlap → setCut succeeds. When overlap = 10s, window = 500ms, 2*window = 1s < 10s. So setCut always succeeds for computed overlaps. The cut==0 with next.started non-zero case only arises if... setCut is called on next's Started with active's plannedEnd — that's overlapEnd. overlapEnd.Sub(overlapStart) < 2*window can happen if the next started very late (near or after active's planned end). Then the switch emits held packets of next with cut==0 — dedup by content is skipped, and active wrote packets up to its end. The next's packets stamped before the active's end were captured by both → duplicates. Since the gap is reported, some data-quality loss is expected, but duplicates are a real overlap issue. Minor.

20. **`handle` retry path**: on next's done with error while active still running → retries++ and resetTimer(1s) — but `c.next = nil` and the timer fires `if c.next == nil && !c.final → startNext`. Wait: startNext is invoked on timer.C when `c.next == nil`. But after a retry the timer is set to 1s. When it fires, `startNext` again. But if the retry exhausts (retries >= captureStartRetries), the done-with-error path returns an error. OK.

But note: after `c.next = nil; resetTimer(timer, time.Second)` — the timer that fired was the next-start timer; fine.

Hmm, wait — there's a potential bug: in `handle`, the retry case returns `(false, nil)` — but the `timer` passed is the run's timer. In `run`, timer.C fires → `if c.next == nil && !c.final { c.startNext(segmentsCtx) }`. Good.

21. **`startNext` resets `c.emitted`, `c.held`, `c.cut`** — but if the previous next is still around? startNext is only called when c.next == nil. OK.

22. **`captureChain.run` — `c.active = c.start(segmentsCtx, ...)`; timer := NewTimer(c.nextStartIn())`. nextStartIn marks final if deadline near. OK.

23. **Deadline handling in `nextStartIn`**: `activeEnd.Before(deadline.Add(-window))` → if active would end after deadline - window, final. So the last segment ends near deadline. OK.

24. **`switchSegments` when final && next == nil → return true** — chain ends. But if final and next != nil (started in time), continues to emit held and switch. OK.

25. **Stopping behavior**: On ctx done, `c.stop(timer)` — closes stdins of active and next. Segments end; their done events → handle → `event.err != nil && !c.stopping` false → not error. active done → switchSegments: stopping && next not started → drop next; `if c.final && c.next == nil → return true`. Wait — `c.final` was set true by stop(). And next dropped to nil. So return true. But what about held packets not yet emitted when cut != 0? In stopping with cut != 0: held packets of next with timestamps... hmm. In switchSegments with stopping: if next.started is zero, drop next & held. If next.started non-zero (cut set), we fall through: `if c.final && c.next == nil` — next != nil → skip; gap report skipped (next.started != 0 and cut != 0); `if c.next != nil && c.next.done && !c.stopping` — stopping → skip; `if c.next == nil` — no; then the held emission loop with cut dedup — good, stopping still writes deduped held packets; then active = next; `if c.active.done → return true`. Good — final packets delivered.

26. **`drain()` on chain return**: consumes events until wg done. But wg done requires the exec goroutine to finish: exec returns when execCtx cancelled (deferred cancel at chain return — wait, `defer cancel()` is segmentsCtx cancel; segmentCtx of the *last* segments derives from segmentsCtx. execCtx is WithoutCancel(segmentCtx), so cancel of segmentCtx does NOT cancel exec. exec goroutine: after stdin closed → clabwire ends → exec returns → closes stdoutWriter → readDone → sends done event → wg.Done. If clabwire doesn't end on stdin close, the watcher goroutine cuts the stream after captureStdinCloseGrace (cancelExec). OK — bounded.

display.text:
# capture command

### Description

The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.

It works with every runtime:

- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).

The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.

--8<-- "docs/cmd/deploy.md:env-vars-flags"

### Usage

`containerlab [global-flags] capture [local-flags]`

### Flags

#### topology | name

Use the global `--topo | -t` flag to reference the lab topology file, or use the global `--name` flag to reference an already deployed lab by name. Without either, containerlab looks for a `*.clab.yml` file in the current directory, like the other lab commands.

With Docker and Podman, the capturable interfaces are the links of the topology file, so `--name` needs the topology file the lab was deployed from to still be in place.

#### target

The local `--target` flag selects what to capture, as `<node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]`. Repeat it for more nodes:

```text
--target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 --target srl2:e1-1
```

The node name ends at the first colon, so interface names such as `1/1/3` or `ethernet-1/1` need no quoting. Node names are accepted as the topology file spells them; with Docker and Podman also as the container name (`clab-srl-srl1`), with c9s also as they were sanitized for Kubernetes (`R1` or `r1`). Interfaces are accepted by their name in the node or by the alias the topology used for them (`e1-1` or `ethernet-1/1` for SR Linux). `--list` shows both.

Only lab link interfaces can be captured; the management interface cannot. An interface that is not a link interface of the node fails the command before anything is captured, and the error lists the node's capturable interfaces.

#### duration

The local `--duration` flag stops the capture after the given time (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). The default `0` captures until the command is interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Captures may run longer than an hour; see [Long captures](#long-captures).

#### packet-limit

The local `--packet-limit` flag stops the capture after that many packets, counted across all targets. `0`, the default, means no limit.

#### snap-length

The local `--snap-length` flag sets how many bytes of each packet are kept, from 64 to 1048576. The default `0` keeps 256 KiB.

#### write

The local `--write | -w` flag names the output file. The default `-` writes to stdout.

#### list

The local `--list` flag lists the interfaces `capture` accepts, for every running node, with the node and interface at the other end of each link, instead of capturing. `--format | -f` selects `table` (default) or `json`.

### Output

The output is one pcapng section:

- a Section Header Block with `shb_userappl` set to `containerlab`
- one Interface Description Block per target, in the order of the `--target` flags, written before any packet: link type Ethernet, the snap length, nanosecond timestamps, and the name `<node>:<interface>` (for example `srl1:e1-1`), with the node named as the topology spells it
- Enhanced Packet Blocks of all targets, in timestamp order: packets are held briefly (100 ms with Docker and Podman, 250 ms with c9s) and written ordered by timestamp, so packets of different interfaces come out in order even though each one is read on its own; a packet that arrives later than that is written as it comes

The interface name shows in Wireshark's interface column (`frame.interface_name`), so a capture of several nodes can be filtered by node and interface.

When the capture ends (duration, packet limit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), the command finishes the stream and exits with code 0; the file is a valid capture. Status messages go to stderr. With c9s, every `clabwire` capture in the pods ends with the command: containerlab closes its stdin, and `clabwire` (`--stop-on-stdin-close`) stops.

`--list -f json` prints an array:

```json
[
  {
    "node": "srl1",
    "interface": "e1-1",
    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
    "peer_node": "srl2",
    "peer_interface": "ethernet-1/1"
  }
]
```

`alias` is present only when the topology used an alias for the interface. `peer_node` is `host` for a host endpoint and `mgmt-net` for a management network endpoint.

### How Docker and Podman captures work

For each target, containerlab enters the node's network namespace, opens a Linux packet socket (`AF_PACKET`) bound to the interface, and leaves the namespace again; the socket keeps capturing on that interface. This is what `tcpdump` does inside the node, without needing `tcpdump` in the node or on the host. All sockets are opened before the first byte is written, so a capture that cannot start (a node that does not run, a missing interface) fails without output.

- Packets carry the kernel's receive timestamps, so packets of different nodes compare on one clock.
- 802.1Q tags, which the kernel keeps outside the frame, are put back in place, so VLAN traffic shows its tags as on the wire.
- Each socket is in promiscuous mode for as long as it is open; the interface returns to its previous state when the capture ends.
- An interface that goes down and up again keeps being captured. When an interface disappears, for example while its node restarts, containerlab waits for it and reattaches once the node is back (`containerlab restart --node`). The time it was gone is reported as a warning with its start and end time.

The command needs root (to open packet sockets and enter network namespaces), as other lab commands do.

### Long captures

Docker and Podman captures have no length limit. With c9s, one `clabwire` capture lasts at most one hour. `capture` chains captures: it starts the next one shortly before the current one ends, lets both run for a few seconds, and switches between them in the middle of that overlap. The repeated section and interface headers of the follow-up are dropped, and packets seen by both captures near the switch are written once (they are matched by content, because each capture stamps packets when it reads them). Once the switch time has passed, the previous capture is stopped through its stdin instead of running to its end. If a follow-up capture does not start in time, the missing interval is reported as a warning with its start and end time; it is never skipped silently. The timestamp order holds across switches: while one node's capture switches, packets of other nodes stamped after the switch wait for it.

### Examples

#### Capture two nodes for 30 seconds into one file

```bash
containerlab capture -t srl.clab.yml \
  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
```

#### Watch a capture live in Wireshark

```bash
containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 -w - | wireshark -k -i -
```

#### Capture the first 100 packets with tshark

```bash
containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:ethernet-1/1 --packet-limit 100 -w - | tshark -r -
```

#### List the capturable interfaces

```bash
containerlab capture --name srl --list
```

#### Capture a c9s lab

```bash
containerlab -r c9s capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 -w srl.pcapng
```

3521: +The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.
3522: +
3523: +It works with every runtime:
3524: +
3525: +- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
3526: +- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).
3527: +
3528: +The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.
3529: +
3530: +--8<-- "docs/cmd/deploy.md:env-vars-flags"
3531: +
3532: +### Usage
3533: +
3534: +`containerlab [global-flags] capture [local-flags]`
3535: +
3536: +### Flags
3537: +
3538: +#### topology | name
3539: +
3540: +Use the global `--topo | -t` flag to reference the lab topology file, or use the global `--name` flag to reference an already deployed lab by name. Without either, containerlab looks for a `*.clab.yml` file in the current directory, like the other lab commands.
3541: +
3542: +With Docker and Podman, the capturable interfaces are the links of the topology file, so `--name` needs the topology file the lab was deployed from to still be in place.
3543: +
3544: +#### target
3545: +
3546: +The local `--target` flag selects what to capture, as `<node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]`. Repeat it for more nodes:
3547: +
3548: +```text
3549: +--target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 --target srl2:e1-1
3550: +```
3551: +
3552: +The node name ends at the first colon, so interface names such as `1/1/3` or `ethernet-1/1` need no quoting. Node names are accepted as the topology file spells them; with Docker and Podman also as the container name (`clab-srl-srl1`), with c9s also as they were sanitized for Kubernetes (`R1` or `r1`). Interfaces are accepted by their name in the node or by the alias the topology used for them (`e1-1` or `ethernet-1/1` for SR Linux). `--list` shows both.
3553: +
3554: +Only lab link interfaces can be captured; the management interface cannot. An interface that is not a link interface of the node fails the command before anything is captured, and the error lists the node's capturable interfaces.
3555: +
3556: +#### duration
3557: +
3558: +The local `--duration` flag stops the capture after the given time (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). The default `0` captures until the command is interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Captures may run longer than an hour; see [Long captures](#long-captures).
3559: +
3560: +#### packet-limit
3561: +
3562: +The local `--packet-limit` flag stops the capture after that many packets, counted across all targets. `0`, the default, means no limit.
3563: +
3564: +#### snap-length
3565: +
3566: +The local `--snap-length` flag sets how many bytes of each packet are kept, from 64 to 1048576. The default `0` keeps 256 KiB.
3567: +
3568: +#### write
3569: +
3570: +The local `--write | -w` flag names the output file. The default `-` writes to stdout.
3571: +
3572: +#### list
3573: +
3574: +The local `--list` flag lists the interfaces `capture` accepts, for every running node, with the node and interface at the other end of each link, instead of capturing. `--format | -f` selects `table` (default) or `json`.
3575: +
3576: +### Output
3577: +
3578: +The output is one pcapng section:
3579: +
3580: +- a Section Header Block with `shb_userappl` set to `containerlab`
3581: +- one Interface Description Block per target, in the order of the `--target` flags, written before any packet: link type Ethernet, the snap length, nanosecond timestamps, and the name `<node>:<interface>` (for example `srl1:e1-1`), with the node named as the topology spells it
3582: +- Enhanced Packet Blocks of all targets, in timestamp order: packets are held briefly (100 ms with Docker and Podman, 250 ms with c9s) and written ordered by timestamp, so packets of different interfaces come out in order even though each one is read on its own; a packet that arrives later than that is written as it comes
3583: +
3584: +The interface name shows in Wireshark's interface column (`frame.interface_name`), so a capture of several nodes can be filtered by node and interface.
3585: +
3586: +When the capture ends (duration, packet limit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), the command finishes the stream and exits with code 0; the file is a valid capture. Status messages go to stderr. With c9s, every `clabwire` capture in the pods ends with the command: containerlab closes its stdin, and `clabwire` (`--stop-on-stdin-close`) stops.

3588: +`--list -f json` prints an array:

3590: +```json
3591: +[
3592: +  {
3593: +    "node": "srl1",
3594: +    "interface": "e1-1",
3595: +    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
3596: +    "peer_node": "srl2",
3597: +    "peer_interface": "ethernet-1/1"
3598: +  }
3599: +]
3600: +```
3601: +
3602: +`alias` is present only when the topology used an alias for the interface. `peer_node` is `host` for a host endpoint and `mgmt-net` for a management network endpoint.
3603: +
3604: +### How Docker and Podman captures work
3605: +
3606: +For each target, containerlab enters the node's network namespace, opens a Linux packet socket (`AF_PACKET`) bound to the interface, and leaves the namespace again; the socket keeps capturing on that interface. This is what `tcpdump` does inside the node, without needing `tcpdump` in the node or on the host. All sockets are opened before the first byte is written, so a capture that cannot start (a node that does not run, a missing interface) fails without output.
3607: +
3608: +- Packets carry the kernel's receive timestamps, so packets of different nodes compare on one clock.
3609: +- 802.1Q tags, which the kernel keeps outside the frame, are put back in place, so VLAN traffic shows its tags as on the wire.
3610: +- Each socket is in promiscuous mode for as long as it is open; the interface returns to its previous state when the capture ends.
3611: +- An interface that goes down and up again keeps being captured. When an interface disappears, for example while its node restarts, containerlab waits for it and reattaches once the node is back (`containerlab restart --node`). The time it was gone is reported as a warning with its start and end time.
3612: +
3613: +The command needs root (to open packet sockets and enter network namespaces), as other lab commands do.
3614: +
3615: +### Long captures
3616: +
3617: +Docker and Podman captures have no length limit. With c9s, one `clabwire` capture lasts at most one hour. `capture` chains captures: it starts the next one shortly before the current one ends, lets both run for a few seconds, and switches between them in the middle of that overlap. The repeated section and interface headers of the follow-up are dropped, and packets seen by both captures near the switch are written once (they are matched by content, because each capture stamps packets when it reads them). Once the switch time has passed, the previous capture is stopped through its stdin instead of running to its end. If a follow-up capture does not start in time, the missing interval is reported as a warning with its start and end time; it is never skipped silently. The timestamp order holds across switches: while one node's capture switches, packets of other nodes stamped after the switch wait for it.

+The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.

+
+- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
+- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).
+
+The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.

+The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.
+
+It works with every runtime:
+
+- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
+- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).
+
+The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.
+
+--8<-- "docs/cmd/deploy.md:env-vars-flags"
+
+### Usage
+
+`containerlab [global-flags] capture [local-flags]`
+
+### Flags
+
+#### topology | name
+
+Use the global `--topo | -t` flag to reference the lab topology file, or use the global `--name` flag to reference an already deployed lab by name. Without either, containerlab looks for a `*.clab.yml` file in the current directory, like the other lab commands.
+
+With Docker and Podman, the capturable interfaces are the links of the topology file, so `--name` needs the topology file the lab was deployed from to still be in place.
+
+#### target
+
+The local `--target` flag selects what to capture, as `<node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]`. Repeat it for more nodes:
+
+```text
+--target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 --target srl2:e1-1
+```
+
+The node name ends at the first colon, so interface names such as `1/1/3` or `ethernet-1/1` need no quoting. Node names are accepted as the topology file spells them; with Docker and Podman also as the container name (`clab-srl-srl1`), with c9s also as they were sanitized for Kubernetes (`R1` or `r1`). Interfaces are accepted by their name in the node or by the alias the topology used for them (`e1-1` or `ethernet-1/1` for SR Linux). `--list` shows both.
+
+Only lab link interfaces can be captured; the management interface cannot. An interface that is not a link interface of the node fails the command before anything is captured, and the error lists the node's capturable interfaces.
+
+#### duration
+
+The local `--duration` flag stops the capture after the given time (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). The default `0` captures until the command is interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Captures may run longer than an hour; see [Long captures](#long-captures).
+
+#### packet-limit
+
+The local `--packet-limit` flag stops the capture after that many packets, counted across all targets. `0`, the default, means no limit.
+
+#### snap-length
+
+The local `--snap-length` flag sets how many bytes of each packet are kept, from 64 to 1048576. The default `0` keeps 256 KiB.
+
+#### write
+
+The local `--write | -w` flag names the output file. The default `-` writes to stdout.
+
+#### list
+
+The local `--list` flag lists the interfaces `capture` accepts, for every running node, with the node and interface at the other end of each link, instead of capturing. `--format | -f` selects `table` (default) or `json`.
+
+### Output
+
+The output is one pcapng section:
+
+- a Section Header Block with `shb_userappl` set to `containerlab`
+- one Interface Description Block per target, in the order of the `--target` flags, written before any packet: link type Ethernet, the snap length, nanosecond timestamps, and the name `<node>:<interface>` (for example `srl1:e1-1`), with the node named as the topology spells it
+- Enhanced Packet Blocks of all targets, in timestamp order: packets are held briefly (100 ms with Docker and Podman, 250 ms with c9s) and written ordered by timestamp, so packets of different interfaces come out in order even though each one is read on its own; a packet that arrives later than that is written as it comes
+
+The interface name shows in Wireshark's interface column (`frame.interface_name`), so a capture of several nodes can be filtered by node and interface.
+
+When the capture ends (duration, packet limit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), the command finishes the stream and exits with code 0; the file is a valid capture. Status messages go to stderr. With c9s, every `clabwire` capture in the pods ends with the command: containerlab closes its stdin, and `clabwire` (`--stop-on-stdin-close`) stops.
+
+`--list -f json` prints an array:
+
+```json
+[
+  {
+    "node": "srl1",
+    "interface": "e1-1",
+    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
+    "peer_node": "srl2",
+    "peer_interface": "ethernet-1/1"
+  }
+]
+```
+
+`alias` is present only when the topology used an alias for the interface. `peer_node` is `host` for a host endpoint and `mgmt-net` for a management network endpoint.
+
+### How Docker and Podman captures work
+
+For each target, containerlab enters the node's network namespace, opens a Linux packet socket (`AF_PACKET`) bound to the interface, and leaves the namespace again; the socket keeps capturing on that interface. This is what `tcpdump` does inside the node, without needing `tcpdump` in the node or on the host. All sockets are opened before the first byte is written, so a capture that cannot start (a node that does not run, a missing interface) fails without output.
+
+- Packets carry the kernel's receive timestamps, so packets of different nodes compare on one clock.
+- 802.1Q tags, which the kernel keeps outside the frame, are put back in place, so VLAN traffic shows its tags as on the wire.
+- Each socket is in promiscuous mode for as long as it is open; the interface returns to its previous state when the capture ends.
+- An interface that goes down and up again keeps being captured. When an interface disappears, for example while its node restarts, containerlab waits for it and reattaches once the node is back (`containerlab restart --node`). The time it was gone is reported as a warning with its start and end time.
+
+The command needs root (to open packet sockets and enter network namespaces), as other lab commands do.
+
+### Long captures
+
+Docker and Podman captures have no length limit. With c9s, one `clabwire` capture lasts at most one hour. `capture` chains captures: it starts the next one shortly before the current one ends, lets both run for a few seconds, and switches between them in the middle of that overlap. The repeated section and interface headers of the follow-up are dropped, and packets seen by both captures near the switch are written once (they are matched by content, because each capture stamps packets when it reads them). Once the switch time has passed, the previous capture is stopped through its stdin instead of running to its end. If a follow-up capture does not start in time, the missing interval is reported as a warning with its start and end time; it is never skipped silently. The timestamp order holds across switches: while one node's capture switches, packets of other nodes stamped after the switch wait for it.
+
+### Examples
+
+#### Capture two nodes for 30 seconds into one file
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture -t srl.clab.yml \
+  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
+```
+
+#### Watch a capture live in Wireshark
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 -w - | wireshark -k -i -
+```
+
+#### Capture the first 100 packets with tshark
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:ethernet-1/1 --packet-limit 100 -w - | tshark -r -
+```
+
+#### List the capturable interfaces
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --list
+```
+
+#### Capture a c9s lab
+
+```bash
+containerlab -r c9s capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 -w srl.pcapng
+```

+[`containerlab capture`](../../cmd/capture.md) captures lab link interfaces of
+one or more nodes into one pcapng stream. Each node's pod runs the `clabwire`

+  per node, with `--nodeName`, every requested interface of that node,
+  `--format pcapng` and `--stop-on-stdin-close`, with stdin attached.

+  target named `<node>:<interface>` (the node as the topology spells it),
+  written before the first packet, and the packets of every target with their
+  interface IDs remapped.
+- Packets are written in timestamp order. Each node's stream arrives over its
+  own exec stream, so the merged stream holds every packet for 250 ms and
+  writes the held packets ordered by timestamp. A packet that arrives later
+  than that, stamped before a packet already written, is written as it comes;
+  the number of such packets goes to the debug log.
+- `clabwire` limits one capture to one hour. Longer captures, and captures
+  without `--duration`, chain captures with a few seconds of overlap and switch
+  in the middle of it; packets near the switch are matched by content so each
+  is written once. A follow-up that does not start in time is reported as a
+  gap, with its time span.

+  `c9s.direct-packet-capture-audit/v1alpha1`) with status `Denied` or `Failed`

447: // Capture streams pcapng from lab link interfaces to w: one section, one Interface Description
448: // Block per target in request order named <node>:<interface>, then the packets of every target.
449: //
450: // Each node's interfaces are captured by one clabwire process in the node's pod. clabwire limits
451: // a capture to one hour, so a longer capture (or one without Duration) chains captures: the next
452: // one starts before the current one ends, and the stream switches at a cut in the overlap. See
453: // captureChain for how packets of the overlap are kept once.
454: //
455: // Packets go out in timestamp order across nodes, through a reorder buffer (captureReorder).
456: //
457: // Every clabwire process runs with stdin attached and --stop-on-stdin-close: a Kubernetes exec
458: // does not stop its process when the stream closes, so containerlab closes stdin whenever a
459: // segment ends (the capture ends, fails, its output fails, or a newer segment took over) and
460: // clabwire ends the capture itself.
461: //
462: // Capture returns when Duration has passed, PacketLimit packets were written, or ctx ends; an
463: // ended ctx is not an error. Every block reaches w in one write, so the stream is a valid capture
464: // whenever it stops. A clabwire Denied or Failed audit record is returned as an error.
465: func (r *Runtime) Capture(
466: 	ctx context.Context,
467: 	req clablabruntime.CaptureRequest,
468: 	w io.Writer,
469: ) error {
470: 	if err := clabcapture.ValidateRequest(&req); err != nil {
471: 		return err
472: 	}
473: 
474: 	r, err := r.connect(ctx, req.Identity)
475: 	if err != nil {
476: 		return err
477: 	}
478: 
479: 	resolved, err := r.resolveCaptureTargets(ctx, req)
480: 	if err != nil {
481: 		return err
482: 	}
483: 
484: 	captureCtx, stop := context.WithCancel(ctx)
485: 	defer stop()
486: 
487: 	out, err := clabcapture.NewOutput(w, resolved.names, req.SnapLength, req.PacketLimit,
488: 		r.captureReorderWindowLength(), stop)
489: 	if err != nil {
490: 		return err
491: 	}
492: 
493: 	run := &captureRun{
494: 		r:       r,
495: 		req:     req,
496: 		out:     out,
497: 		segment: r.captureSegmentLength(),
498: 	}
499: 	if req.Duration > 0 {
500: 		run.deadline = time.Now().Add(req.Duration)
501: 	}
502: 	run.overlap = min(maxCaptureOverlap, run.segment/3)
503: 	run.window = min(maxCaptureCutWindow, run.overlap/4)
504: 
505: 	if req.Duration > 0 {
506: 		// a clabwire process that does not end on its own does not hold the capture open
507: 		var cancelTimeout context.CancelFunc
508: 		captureCtx, cancelTimeout = context.WithTimeout(captureCtx,
509: 			req.Duration+run.overlap+captureEndGrace)
510: 		defer cancelTimeout()
511: 	}
512: 
513: 	group, groupCtx := errgroup.WithContext(captureCtx)
514: 	for _, captureGroup := range resolved.groups {
515: 		chain := &captureChain{capture: run, group: captureGroup}
516: 		group.Go(func() error {
517: 			return chain.run(groupCtx)
518: 		})
519: 	}
520: 
521: 	err = group.Wait()
522: 	if writeErr := out.Close(); writeErr != nil {
523: 		return writeErr
524: 	}
525: 	if err != nil && !(errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) && captureCtx.Err() != nil) {
526: 		return err
527: 	}
528: 
529: 	return nil
530: }

586: // captureChain runs the chained clabwire captures of one group.
587: //
588: // Chaining and the cut: segment k+1 starts `overlap` before segment k is due to end, so both
589: // capture the same packets for a while. clabwire stamps packets when it reads them, so two
590: // processes give the same packet timestamps a few microseconds apart, and timestamps alone
591: // cannot pair them. The chain therefore cuts in the middle of the overlap and matches packets by
592: // content close to the cut:
593: //
594: //  1. When segment k+1 reports Started (pod clock, from its audit record), the cut is
595: //     T = midpoint of [Started(k+1), Started(k) + duration(k)]: both segments run then.
596: //  2. Segment k keeps streaming live, but only packets stamped before T; it remembers the
597: //     content of what it wrote since segment k+1 started.
598: //  3. Segment k+1's packets are held back until segment k has ended. Then the ones stamped
599: //     before T-W are dropped (segment k had them), the ones stamped within W of T are dropped
600: //     when segment k wrote the same bytes on the same interface, and every other one is written.
601: //     From then on segment k+1 streams live.
602: //
603: // Once the pod clock passed T+W, segment k's stdin is closed so it ends without running to its
604: // planned end. While packets are held back, the chain holds the reorder buffer at T-W, so other
605: // nodes' later packets do not overtake them in the merged stream.
606: //
607: // W (500 ms, less for short test segments) covers the stamping difference. Identical frames on
608: // the same interface within W of the cut can be paired with each other, which can drop a true
609: // repeat; nothing else is lost or doubled. A follow-up segment that does not start in time leaves
610: // a gap, which is reported through CaptureRequest.OnGap (or logged), never silently ignored.
611: type captureChain struct {
612: 	capture *captureRun
613: 	group   *captureGroup
614: 
615: 	events chan segmentEvent
616: 	wg     sync.WaitGroup
617: 
618: 	active *captureSegment
619: 	next   *captureSegment
620: 	// cut is the switch time between active and next, in nanoseconds; zero until known.
621: 	cut int64
622: 	// emitted remembers the content of the packets active wrote while next runs.
623: 	emitted map[uint64]int
624: 	// held are the packets of next until active ends.
625: 	held     []*clabcapture.Packet
626: 	segments int
627: 	retries  int
628: 	// final is set once no further segment is due.
629: 	final bool
630: 	// stopping is set once ctx ended: the segments are asked to end and what they still
631: 	// deliver is written.
632: 	stopping bool
633: }
634: 
635: // run runs the chain until its last segment ended. When ctx ends, it stops the segments and
636: // keeps writing the packets they read until then; a segment that does not end within
637: // captureStdinCloseGrace is cut.
638: func (c *captureChain) run(ctx context.Context) error {
639: 	c.events = make(chan segmentEvent, 256)
640: 	// the segments outlive ctx so they can deliver their last packets; segmentsCtx cuts them
641: 	segmentsCtx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.WithoutCancel(ctx))
642: 	var abort *time.Timer
643: 	defer func() {
644: 		if abort != nil {
645: 			abort.Stop()
646: 		}
647: 		cancel()
648: 		c.drain()
649: 		c.capture.out.Release(c)
650: 	}()
651: 
652: 	c.active = c.start(segmentsCtx, c.segmentDuration(time.Now()))
653: 	timer := time.NewTimer(c.nextStartIn())
654: 	defer timer.Stop()
655: 
656: 	done := ctx.Done()
657: 	for {
658: 		select {
659: 		case <-done:
660: 			done = nil
661: 			c.stop(timer)
662: 			abort = time.AfterFunc(captureStdinCloseGrace, cancel)
663: 		case <-segmentsCtx.Done():
664: 			return nil
665: 		case <-timer.C:
666: 			if c.next == nil && !c.final {
667: 				c.startNext(segmentsCtx)
668: 			}
669: 		case event := <-c.events:
670: 			stop, err := c.handle(segmentsCtx, event, timer)
671: 			if err != nil || stop {
672: 				return err
673: 			}
674: 		}
675: 	}
676: }
677:

679: // ones are asked to end. The chain then writes what they deliver until they ended.

121: // stop is called once the packet limit is reached or a write failed. Close must be called.
122: func NewOutput(

124: 	names []string,
125: 	snapLength, packetLimit int,
126: 	window time.Duration,
127: 	stop func(),
128: ) (*Output, error) {

132: 		uint32(snapLength),
133: 	); err != nil { //nolint:gosec // validated
134: 		return nil, err
135: 	}

137: 	out := &Output{

139: 		reorder: NewReorder(window, writer.WritePacket, stop),
140: 		limit:   int64(packetLimit),
141: 		stop:    stop,
142: 		runDone: make(chan struct{}),

156: // once the packet limit is reached and the capture stops, and returns the error of a failed
157: // write.

171: 		}
172: 
173: 		return true, nil
174: 	}
175: 
176: 	o.written.Add(1)
177: 
178: 	return true, o.reorder.Push(id, packet)
179: }

Analysis of reorder.go / output.go:

**Issue A — `Output.Close` calls `Flush` after `Run` returned, but `Run` may return while `writeDue` still returns a due time.** No — Run returns only on ctx done. Close then Flush writes remaining. Fine.

**Issue B — `Reorder.Push` blocking**: `Push` takes q.mu; `writeDue` holds q.mu while calling `writeLocked` → `write` = `writer.WritePacket` → writer (to w). If w is a slow pipe, writeDue holds the lock for the duration of the write, blocking all Push calls. Backpressure is intended. But note: c9s chain `send` blocks when events channel full (256). Reader goroutines blocked on send. That's the backpressure chain. OK.

**Issue C — `Reorder.Flush` doesn't wake; fine since called after Run ended.**

But wait — there's a real subtlety: `Output.Close` cancels run and waits, then Flush. However, `Emit` may be called concurrently with `Close`? In c9s, chains have exited (group.Wait) before out.Close. In local, wg.Wait before out.Close. OK.

**Issue D — `Output.Emit` with limit: `count > o.limit` → stop and return (false, nil). But this packet is dropped and not counted... it was counted (written.Add). Fine.

**Issue E — cursor and late packets**: `q.cursor` updated only via popLocked. Late direct writes don't update cursor — but a late packet has Timestamp < cursor, so max() wouldn't change. Fine. But consider window > 0 and a hold: while held, head.timestamp > limit → return zero time; wait = 1 hour; on Release → wake. OK.

**Issue F — `writeDue` returns `due` (next due time) even when the head is behind a hold?** No — it checks hold first: if held && head.ts > limit → return zero (no wake until release). But what if head.ts <= limit and due in future → returns due. Good.

**Issue G — packet with Timestamp == 0?** c9s packets always have timestamps from clabwire. Local packets from afpacket have kernel timestamps. OK.

**Issue H — `Push` when `q.err != nil` returns error. Local reader drains and closes; c9s `send` of packet events continues but handlePacket → emit → Push returns err → chain returns err. But if chain already returned... The chain returns error from handle → run returns err → group.Wait returns first error → Capture returns err (unless ctx canceled). For a write failure (Wireshark closed), stop() cancels captureCtx → groupCtx canceled → other chains stop. Good.

**Issue I — Race on `Output.Close` vs pending `Push` after error?** After a write error, chains stop; group.Wait returns; out.Close called. No more Push. OK.

**Issue J — In `Output.Emit`, when `count == o.limit` → stop() and return false — the packet WAS pushed (Push before the check). Good: the limit-th packet is written.

**Issue K — `Written()` used by c9s `start` for `remaining` computation — reads atomic; races with concurrent Emit from other chains; benign (close enough; min with 1).

95: 		window:         localReorderWindow,

104: 	reopenInterval time.Duration

108: 	ctx context.Context,

110: 	targets []LocalTarget,
111: 	w io.Writer,
112: ) error {

114: 		return err
115: 	}
116: 	if len(targets) != len(req.Targets) {
117: 		return fmt.Errorf("capture has %d resolved targets for %d requested ones",

119: 	}

121: 	sources, err := l.openAll(ctx, targets, req.SnapLength)
122: 	if err != nil {

124: 	}
125: 
126: 	names := make([]string, len(targets))
127: 	for idx, target := range targets {

129: 	}

140: 	if err != nil {

143: 		}
144: 
145: 		return err
146: 	}

148: 	var wg sync.WaitGroup
149: 	for idx, source := range sources {
150: 		reader := &localReader{
151: 			capture: l,
152: 			out:     out,

167: // openAll opens the sockets of every target before anything is written, one namespace entry
168: // per node, so a capture that cannot start fails without output.
169: func (l localCapture) openAll(
170: 	ctx context.Context,
171: 	targets []LocalTarget,
172: 	snapLength int,
173: ) ([]packetSource, error) {
174: 	type nodeTargets struct {
175: 		exec    ExecFunc
176: 		indexes []int
177: 		names   []string
178: 	}

180: 	byNode := map[string]*nodeTargets{}

182: 		group := byNode[target.Node]

185: 			byNode[target.Node] = group
186: 			order = append(order, target.Node)

188: 		group.indexes = append(group.indexes, idx)
189: 		group.names = append(group.names, target.Interface)
190: 	}

192: 	sources := make([]packetSource, len(targets))
193: 	closeAll := func() {
194: 		for _, source := range sources {
195: 			if source != nil {
196: 				source.Close()
197: 			}
198: 		}
199: 	}
200: 	for _, node := range order {
201: 		group := byNode[node]
202: 		opened, err := l.open(ctx, group.exec, group.names, snapLength)
203: 		if err != nil {
204: 			closeAll()

207: 		for idx, source := range opened {

212: 	return sources, nil

216: type localReader struct {
217: 	capture localCapture
218: 	out     *Output
219: 	id      uint32
220: 	target  LocalTarget

226: 	defer func() {
227: 		if source != nil {
228: 			source.Close()
229: 		}
230: 	}()
231: 
232: 	for {
233: 		if ctx.Err() != nil {

236: 		}

241: 		}
242: 		if err != nil {

249: 			if source == nil {
250: 				return
251: 			}
252: 
253: 			continue
254: 		}
255: 
256: 		if more, err := r.out.Emit(r.id, r.packet(data, info)); !more || err != nil {
257: 			return
258: 		}
259: 	}
260: }

262: // drain writes the packets that arrived before end but were still in the socket's ring: the
263: // kernel hands over a ring block once it is full or its block timeout passed, so the last
264: // packets before a capture ended may not have been read yet.
265: func (r *localReader) drain(source packetSource, end time.Time) {
266: 	deadline := end.Add(localDrainTimeout)
267: 	for time.Now().Before(deadline) {
268: 		data, info, err := source.ReadPacket()
269: 		if errors.Is(err, errReadTimeout) && time.Since(end) < localDrainQuiet {
270: 			continue
271: 		}
272: 		if err != nil || info.Timestamp.After(end) {
273: 			return
274: 		}
275: 		if more, err := r.out.Emit(r.id, r.packet(data, info)); !more || err != nil {
276: 			return
277: 		}
278: 	}
279: }

281: // packet copies a packet out of the socket's ring, cut to the snap length.
282: func (r *localReader) packet(data []byte, info gopacket.CaptureInfo) *Packet {
283: 	length := info.Length
284: 	for _, ancillary := range info.AncillaryData {
285: 		if _, ok := ancillary.(afpacket.AncillaryVLAN); ok {
286: 			// the tag was put back into the data and counts toward the frame length
287: 			length += vlanHeaderLength
288: 			break
289: 		}
290: 	}
291: 	length = max(length, len(data))
292: 
293: 	captured := make([]byte, min(len(data), r.snap))
294: 	copy(captured, data)
295: 
296: 	return &Packet{
297: 		Timestamp:      info.Timestamp.UnixNano(),
298: 		OriginalLength: uint32(length), //nolint:gosec // bounded by the interface MTU
299: 		Data:           captured,
300: 	}
301: }

303: // reopen opens the interface's socket again once its node and interface are back. It returns
304: // nil when the capture ended first. Time the interface could not be opened is reported as a gap;
305: // an interface that only went down is not, as it has no traffic while down.
306: func (r *localReader) reopen(ctx context.Context) packetSource {
307: 	from := time.Now()
308: 	var unavailable error
309: 
310: 	timer := time.NewTimer(r.capture.reopenInterval)
311: 	defer timer.Stop()
312: 
313: 	for {
314: 		select {
315: 		case <-ctx.Done():
316: 			if unavailable != nil {
317: 				r.reportGap(from, time.Time{}, unavailable)
318: 			}
319: 
320: 			return nil
321: 		case <-timer.C:
322: 		}
323: 
324: 		opened, err := r.capture.open(ctx, r.target.Exec, []string{r.target.Interface}, r.snap)
325: 		if err != nil {
326: 			if unavailable == nil {
327: 				log.Debug("Capture interface is not available, waiting for it",
328: 					"node", r.target.Node, "interface", r.target.Interface, "error", err)
329: 			}
330: 			unavailable = err
331: 			resetTimer(timer, r.capture.reopenInterval)
332: 
333: 			continue
334: 		}
335: 		if unavailable != nil {
336: 			r.reportGap(from, time.Now(), unavailable)
337: 		}
338: 
339: 		return opened[0]
340: 	}
341: }
342: 
343: func (r *localReader) reportGap(from, to time.Time, cause error) {
344: 	ReportGap(r.onGap, clablabruntime.CaptureGap{
345: 		Node:       r.target.Node,
346: 		Interfaces: []string{r.target.Interface},
347: 		From:       from,
348: 		To:         to,
349: 		Reason:     fmt.Sprintf("the interface was not available: %v", cause),
350: 	})
351: }

353: // openPacketSockets opens one packet socket per interface in the namespace exec enters. A socket
354: // stays bound to its interface after the thread left the namespace.
355: func openPacketSockets(
356: 	ctx context.Context,
357: 	exec ExecFunc,
358: 	interfaces []string,
359: 	snapLength int,
360: ) ([]packetSource, error) {
361: 	sources := make([]packetSource, 0, len(interfaces))
362: 	err := exec(ctx, func(ns.NetNS) error {
363: 		for _, name := range interfaces {
364: 			source, err := openPacketSocket(name, snapLength)
365: 			if err != nil {
366: 				return fmt.Errorf("interface %q: %w", name, err)
367: 			}
368: 			sources = append(sources, source)
369: 		}
370: 
371: 		return nil
372: 	})
373: 	if err != nil {
374: 		for _, source := range sources {
375: 			source.Close()
376: 		}
377: 
378: 		return nil, err
379: 	}
380: 
381: 	return sources, nil
382: }

384: // afpacketSource is a TPACKET_V3 receive ring on one interface.
385: type afpacketSource struct {
386: 	handle *afpacket.TPacket
387: }
388: 
389: func openPacketSocket(name string, snapLength int) (*afpacketSource, error) {
390: 	// A TPACKET_V3 block holds whole frames: it must be larger than the snap length, plus the
391: 	// block and frame headers, and a multiple of the page size.
392: 	pageSize := os.Getpagesize()
393: 	blockSize := max(localMinBlockSize, snapLength+pageSize)
394: 	blockSize = (blockSize + pageSize - 1) / pageSize * pageSize
395: 
396: 	handle, err := afpacket.NewTPacket(
397: 		afpacket.OptInterface(name),
398: 		afpacket.OptTPacketVersion(afpacket.TPacketVersion3),
399: 		afpacket.OptFrameSize(blockSize),
400: 		afpacket.OptBlockSize(blockSize),
401: 		afpacket.OptNumBlocks(localRingBlocks),
402: 		afpacket.OptBlockTimeout(localBlockTimeout),
403: 		afpacket.OptPollTimeout(localPollTimeout),
404: 		// the kernel moves 802.1Q tags out of the frame; captures show them in place
405: 		afpacket.OptAddVLANHeader(true),
406: 	)
407: 	if err != nil {
408: 		return nil, err
409: 	}
410: 	// promiscuous mode is a membership of this socket and ends with it
411: 	if err := handle.SetPromiscuous(true); err != nil {
412: 		handle.Close()
413: 		return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to enable promiscuous mode: %w", err)
414: 	}
415: 
416: 	return &afpacketSource{handle: handle}, nil
417: }

Verification of local.go concerns:

1. **`openAll` count assumption**: `opened` from `l.open` — openPacketSockets returns exactly len(interfaces) sources on success (appends per interface, and error aborts). So `sources[group.indexes[idx]]` is safe. In tests, `open` is a stub — fine.

2. **`drain` deadline**: `deadline := end.Add(localDrainTimeout)` — end is `time.Now()` at ctx check. Loop condition `time.Now().Before(deadline)`. Inside, `errReadTimeout && time.Since(end) < localDrainQuiet` → continue. Once beyond quiet, errReadTimeout → falls to `if err != nil` → return. Wait: errReadTimeout is an err — `if err != nil || info.Timestamp.After(end)` → return. So after quiet period, drain returns. Good.

Note: `drain` is called with `time.Now()` — but the ctx check happens at loop top; packets read before... fine.

3. **`drain` after packet limit stop**: Emit returns !more → return. OK.

4. **`run` after `reopen` returns nil (ctx done)**: returns. OK.

5. **`reopen` blocks on timer only — checks ctx.Done only every reopenInterval (200ms). Acceptable.

6. **`r.reopen(ctx)` uses `r.capture.open` with ctx — openPacketSockets with a canceled ctx: exec(ctx...) → ns.WithNetNS? presumably fails fast or blocks until ctx... Actually `node.ExecFunction` wraps ns.WithNetNS which doesn't take ctx? ExecFunc signature is `func(ctx context.Context, f func(ns.NetNS) error) error` — hmm, if the underlying exec ignores ctx, reopening in a loop every 200ms until ctx done. Fine.

7. **CaptureInfo.Timestamp**: afpacket ZeroCopyReadPacketData returns the kernel timestamp. Good.

8. **`packet()` length**: `length = info.Length` (original wire length, without the moved-out VLAN tag) + 4 per ancillary VLAN. But if OptAddVLANHeader is on, does `len(data)` include the reinserted tag and info.Length not? They handle that. OK.

1: // Package capture writes the pcapng streams of `containerlab capture`: one section with one
2: // interface per capture target, packets merged across targets in timestamp order. The local
3: // capturer reads lab link interfaces of Docker and Podman nodes through packet sockets; the c9s
4: // lab runtime feeds the same writer from clabwire streams.
5: package capture

17: // pcapng block layout (https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html). clabwire
18: // writes little-endian sections, and so does the merged stream containerlab writes.
19: const (
20: 	pcapngSectionHeaderType  = 0x0a0d0d0a
21: 	pcapngInterfaceType      = 0x00000001
22: 	pcapngEnhancedPacketType = 0x00000006
23: 	pcapngByteOrderMagic     = 0x1a2b3c4d
24: 	pcapngOptionEnd          = 0
25: 	pcapngOptionUserAppl     = 4
26: 	pcapngOptionIfName       = 2
27: 	pcapngOptionIfTSResol    = 9
28: 	pcapngLinkTypeEthernet   = 1

30: 	pcapngNanoseconds = 9
31: 	// pcapngMaxBlockLength bounds a block read from a capture stream: a packet of the largest
32: 	// clabwire snap length (1 MiB) plus framing.
33: 	pcapngMaxBlockLength = 1<<20 + 1024
34: 	// captureUserApplication names the writer in the merged section header.

154: func parsePCAPNGInterface(body []byte) (InterfaceDescription, error) {
155: 	if len(body) < 8 {
156: 		return InterfaceDescription{}, fmt.Errorf("short pcapng interface description")
157: 	}
158: 	intf := InterfaceDescription{
159: 		LinkType:   binary.LittleEndian.Uint16(body[0:2]),
160: 		SnapLength: binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(body[4:8]),
161: 		TSResol:    6,
162: 	}

164: 	options := body[8:]
165: 	for len(options) >= 4 {
166: 		code := binary.LittleEndian.Uint16(options[0:2])
167: 		size := int(binary.LittleEndian.Uint16(options[2:4]))
168: 		if code == pcapngOptionEnd {

170: 		}
171: 		padded := size + pcapngPadding(size)
172: 		if 4+padded > len(options) {
173: 			return InterfaceDescription{}, fmt.Errorf("truncated pcapng interface option")

176: 		switch code {
177: 		case pcapngOptionIfName:

184: 		options = options[4+padded:]

220: // Only decimal resolutions up to nanoseconds occur in clabwire streams.
221: func pcapngNanosecondsFrom(raw uint64, tsresol byte) (int64, error) {

226: 	for range pcapngNanoseconds - int(tsresol) {

228: 	}

255: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint16(section[4:], 1)
256: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint16(section[6:], 0)
257: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint64(section[8:], math.MaxUint64)
258: 	section = appendPCAPNGOption(section, pcapngOptionUserAppl, []byte(captureUserApplication))
259: 	section = appendPCAPNGOption(section, pcapngOptionEnd, nil)
260: 
261: 	header := pcapngBlock(pcapngSectionHeaderType, section)
262: 	for _, name := range names {
263: 		description := make([]byte, 8)
264: 		binary.LittleEndian.PutUint16(description[0:], pcapngLinkTypeEthernet)
265: 		binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(description[4:], snapLength)
266: 		description = appendPCAPNGOption(description, pcapngOptionIfName, []byte(name))
267: 		description = appendPCAPNGOption(description, pcapngOptionIfTSResol,
268: 			[]byte{pcapngNanoseconds})
269: 		description = appendPCAPNGOption(description, pcapngOptionEnd, nil)
270: 		header = append(header, pcapngBlock(pcapngInterfaceType, description)...)
271: 	}

273: 	return p.write(header)

277: func (p *Writer) WritePacket(interfaceID uint32, packet *Packet) error {
278: 	timestamp := uint64(packet.Timestamp) //nolint:gosec // capture timestamps are positive
279: 	body := make([]byte, 20, 20+len(packet.Data)+3)
280: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(body[0:], interfaceID)
281: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(body[4:], uint32(timestamp>>32))
282: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(body[8:], uint32(timestamp)) //nolint:gosec // low 32 bits
283: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(body[12:], uint32(len(packet.Data)))
284: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(body[16:], packet.OriginalLength)
285: 	body = append(body, packet.Data...)
286: 	body = append(body, make([]byte, pcapngPadding(len(packet.Data)))...)

288: 	return p.write(pcapngBlock(pcapngEnhancedPacketType, body))

305: 	}

307: 		p.err = fmt.Errorf("failed to write the capture: %w", err)

310: 	return p.err

314: 	total := uint32(12 + len(body)) //nolint:gosec // bounded by the snap length
315: 	block := make([]byte, 8, total)
316: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(block[0:], blockType)
317: 	binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(block[4:], total)
318: 	block = append(block, body...)
319: 
320: 	return binary.LittleEndian.AppendUint32(block, total)
321: }

324: 	body = binary.LittleEndian.AppendUint16(body, code)

326: 	body = append(body, value...)
327: 
328: 	return append(body, make([]byte, pcapngPadding(len(value)))...)
329: }

+	// localReorderWindow is how long the merged stream holds packets of local sockets back to
+	// write them in timestamp order. Each socket hands over its packets within
+	// localBlockTimeout, so a few times that covers the delivery skew between sockets.
+	localReorderWindow = 100 * time.Millisecond
+	// localBlockTimeout is how long the kernel fills a ring block before it hands it over.
+	localBlockTimeout = 10 * time.Millisecond
+	// localPollTimeout is how often a socket reader checks whether the capture ended.
+	localPollTimeout = 100 * time.Millisecond

+	// that went down or disappeared.
+	localReopenInterval = 200 * time.Millisecond
+	// localDrainQuiet is how long after the end of a capture a reader keeps waiting for packets
+	// still in the socket's ring: the kernel hands over a block within two block timeouts.
+	localDrainQuiet = 5 * localBlockTimeout
+	// localDrainTimeout bounds the drain while packets keep arriving.
+	localDrainTimeout = 250 * time.Millisecond
+	// localRingBlocks and localMinBlockSize size the receive ring of each socket: eight blocks
+	// of at least 1 MiB, each larger than the snap length.
+	localRingBlocks   = 8
+	localMinBlockSize = 1 << 20
+	// vlanHeaderLength is the length of the 802.1Q tag put back into frames whose tag the
+	// kernel moved out of band.
+	vlanHeaderLength = 4
+)
+
+// errReadTimeout is returned by a packet source that has no packet within the poll timeout.
+var errReadTimeout = errors.New("no packet within the poll timeout")
+
+// ExecFunc runs f in the network namespace of a node.
+type ExecFunc func(ctx context.Context, f func(ns.NetNS) error) error
+
+// LocalTarget is one interface of a node on this machine (Docker or Podman) to capture.
+type LocalTarget struct {
+	// Node is the node name as the topology spells it.
+	Node string
+	// Interface is the interface name inside the node.
+	Interface string
+	// Exec runs a function in the node's network namespace.
+	Exec ExecFunc
+}

+	// ReadPacket returns the next packet; the data is only valid until the next call. It

+	ReadPacket() ([]byte, gopacket.CaptureInfo, error)
+	Close()
+}

+	ctx context.Context,
+	exec ExecFunc,
+	interfaces []string,
+	snapLength int,
+) ([]packetSource, error)

+// timestamp order. targets lists the interfaces of req.Targets, resolved, in the same order.

+// the right to enter the namespace, so root. An interface that goes down is reopened once it is
+// up again; one that disappears (its node stopped or was recreated) is reattached when it is
+// back, and the time it was gone is reported as a gap through req.OnGap (or logged).
+func CaptureLocal(
+	ctx context.Context,
+	req clablabruntime.CaptureRequest,
+	targets []LocalTarget,
+	w io.Writer,
+) error {

+		open:           openPacketSockets,
+		window:         localReorderWindow,
+		reopenInterval: localReopenInterval,
+	}.run(ctx, req, targets, w)

+	window         time.Duration
+	reopenInterval time.Duration

+	}

+		return err
+	}

+		var cancelTimeout context.CancelFunc
+		captureCtx, cancelTimeout = context.WithTimeout(captureCtx, req.Duration)
+		defer cancelTimeout()
+	}

+	if err != nil {

+// openAll opens the sockets of every target before anything is written, one namespace entry
+// per node, so a capture that cannot start fails without output.
+func (l localCapture) openAll(
+	ctx context.Context,
+	targets []LocalTarget,
+	snapLength int,

+		exec    ExecFunc
+		indexes []int
+		names   []string
+	}

+		group := byNode[target.Node]
+		if group == nil {
+			group = &nodeTargets{exec: target.Exec}
+			byNode[target.Node] = group
+			order = append(order, target.Node)
+		}
+		group.indexes = append(group.indexes, idx)
+		group.names = append(group.names, target.Interface)

+		}

+// localReader reads one interface into the merged stream.
+type localReader struct {

+func (r *localReader) run(ctx context.Context, source packetSource) {
+	defer func() {

+			source.Close()

+			continue

+// kernel hands over a ring block once it is full or its block timeout passed, so the last
+// packets before a capture ended may not have been read yet.
+func (r *localReader) drain(source packetSource, end time.Time) {
+	deadline := end.Add(localDrainTimeout)

+// packet copies a packet out of the socket's ring, cut to the snap length.
+func (r *localReader) packet(data []byte, info gopacket.CaptureInfo) *Packet {
+	length := info.Length

2279: +func captureFn(cmd *cobra.Command, o *Options) error {
2280: +	if o.Global.TopologyName == "" && o.Global.TopologyFile == "" {
2281: +		return fmt.Errorf("provide either a lab name (--name) or a topology file path (--topo)")
2282: +	}
2283: +
2284: +	if o.Capture.List {
2285: +		return captureListFn(cmd, o)
2286: +	}
2287: +
2288: +	targets, err := parseCaptureTargets(o.Capture.Targets)
2289: +	if err != nil {
2290: +		return err
2291: +	}
2292: +
2293: +	c, err := clabcore.NewContainerLab(o.ToClabOptions()...)
2294: +	if err != nil {
2295: +		return err
2296: +	}
2297: +
2298: +	// An interrupt ends the capture; the command still finishes the file and exits cleanly.
2299: +	// Armed before the file is created, so an interrupt never leaves it empty.
2300: +	o.Global.FinishOnCancel.Store(true)
2301: +	defer o.Global.FinishOnCancel.Store(false)
2302: +
2303: +	output := cmd.OutOrStdout()
2304: +	if o.Capture.Write != "" && o.Capture.Write != "-" {
2305: +		file, err := os.Create(o.Capture.Write)
2306: +		if err != nil {
2307: +			return fmt.Errorf("failed to create the capture file: %w", err)
2308: +		}
2309: +		defer file.Close()
2310: +		output = file
2311: +
2312: +		// the file belongs to the user who ran the command, also through sudo or setuid
2313: +		if err := clabutils.SetUIDAndGID(o.Capture.Write); err != nil {
2314: +			log.Debug("Cannot hand the capture file to the user", "file", o.Capture.Write,
2315: +				"error", err)
2316: +		}
2317: +	}
2318: +
2319: +	err = c.Capture(cmd.Context(), clablabruntime.CaptureRequest{
2320: +		Targets:     targets,
2321: +		Duration:    o.Capture.Duration,
2322: +		PacketLimit: o.Capture.PacketLimit,
2323: +		SnapLength:  o.Capture.SnapLength,
2324: +	}, output)
2325: +	if err != nil {
2326: +		return err
2327: +	}
2328: +
2329: +	if file, ok := output.(*os.File); ok && output != cmd.OutOrStdout() {
2330: +		if err := file.Sync(); err != nil {

2332: +		}

2335: +	return nil
2336: +}

2338: +// parseCaptureTargets parses --target values: <node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]. The node name
2339: +// ends at the first colon, so interface names may contain colons or slashes.
2340: +func parseCaptureTargets(values []string) ([]clablabruntime.CaptureTarget, error) {
2341: +	if len(values) == 0 {
2342: +		return nil, fmt.Errorf("provide at least one --target <node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]")
2343: +	}
2344: +
2345: +	targets := make([]clablabruntime.CaptureTarget, 0, len(values))
2346: +	for _, value := range values {
2347: +		node, interfaces, ok := strings.Cut(strings.TrimSpace(value), ":")
2348: +		node = strings.TrimSpace(node)
2349: +		if !ok || node == "" || strings.TrimSpace(interfaces) == "" {
2350: +			return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid --target %q: use <node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]",
2351: +				value)
2352: +		}
2353: +
2354: +		for _, name := range strings.Split(interfaces, ",") {
2355: +			name = strings.TrimSpace(name)
2356: +			if name == "" {
2357: +				return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid --target %q: empty interface name", value)
2358: +			}
2359: +			targets = append(targets, clablabruntime.CaptureTarget{Node: node, Interface: name})
2360: +		}
2361: +	}
2362: +
2363: +	return targets, nil
2364: +}

2366: +func captureListFn(cmd *cobra.Command, o *Options) error {

2372: +		return fmt.Errorf("output format %q is not supported, use 'table' or 'json'", format)
2373: +	}
2374: +	if len(o.Capture.Targets) != 0 {
2375: +		return fmt.Errorf("--list lists every running node's interfaces; it takes no --target")
2376: +	}
2377: +
2378: +	c, err := clabcore.NewContainerLab(o.ToClabOptions()...)
2379: +	if err != nil {
2380: +		return err
2381: +	}
2382: +
2383: +	interfaces, err := c.CaptureInterfaces(cmd.Context())

2391: +func printCaptureInterfaces(
2392: +	w io.Writer,
2393: +	interfaces []clablabruntime.CaptureInterface,
2394: +	format string,
2395: +) error {
2396: +	if format == clabconstants.FormatJSON {

2398: +			interfaces = []clablabruntime.CaptureInterface{}
2399: +		}
2400: +		data, err := json.MarshalIndent(interfaces, "", "  ")
2401: +		if err != nil {
2402: +			return err
2403: +		}
2404: +		_, err = fmt.Fprintln(w, string(data))
2405: +
2406: +		return err
2407: +	}
2408: +
2409: +	table := tableWriter.NewWriter()
2410: +	table.SetOutputMirror(w)
2411: +	table.SetStyle(tableWriter.StyleRounded)
2412: +	table.Style().Format.Header = text.FormatTitle
2413: +	table.Style().Format.HeaderAlign = text.AlignCenter
2414: +	table.AppendHeader(tableWriter.Row{"Node", "Interface", "Alias", "Peer Node", "Peer Interface"})
2415: +	table.SetColumnConfigs([]tableWriter.ColumnConfig{{Number: 1, AutoMerge: true}})
2416: +	for _, intf := range interfaces {
2417: +		alias := intf.Alias
2418: +		if alias == "" {
2419: +			alias = clabconstants.NotApplicable
2420: +		}
2421: +		table.AppendRow(tableWriter.Row{
2422: +			intf.Node, intf.Interface, alias, intf.PeerNode, intf.PeerInterface,
2423: +		})
2424: +	}
2425: +	table.Render()
2426: +
2427: +	return nil
2428: +}
