3517: +# capture command
3518: +
3519: +### Description
3520: +
3521: +The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.
3522: +
3523: +It works with every runtime:
3524: +
3525: +- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
3526: +- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).
3527: +
3528: +The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.
3529: +
3530: +--8<-- "docs/cmd/deploy.md:env-vars-flags"
3531: +
3532: +### Usage
3533: +
3534: +`containerlab [global-flags] capture [local-flags]`
3535: +
3536: +### Flags
3537: +
3538: +#### topology | name
3539: +
3540: +Use the global `--topo | -t` flag to reference the lab topology file, or use the global `--name` flag to reference an already deployed lab by name. Without either, containerlab looks for a `*.clab.yml` file in the current directory, like the other lab commands.
3541: +
3542: +With Docker and Podman, the capturable interfaces are the links of the topology file, so `--name` needs the topology file the lab was deployed from to still be in place.
3543: +
3544: +#### target
3545: +
3546: +The local `--target` flag selects what to capture, as `<node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]`. Repeat it for more nodes:
3547: +
3548: +```text
3549: +--target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 --target srl2:e1-1
3550: +```
3551: +
3552: +The node name ends at the first colon, so interface names such as `1/1/3` or `ethernet-1/1` need no quoting. Node names are accepted as the topology file spells them; with Docker and Podman also as the container name (`clab-srl-srl1`), with c9s also as they were sanitized for Kubernetes (`R1` or `r1`). Interfaces are accepted by their name in the node or by the alias the topology used for them (`e1-1` or `ethernet-1/1` for SR Linux). `--list` shows both.
3553: +
3554: +Only lab link interfaces can be captured; the management interface cannot. An interface that is not a link interface of the node fails the command before anything is captured, and the error lists the node's capturable interfaces.
3555: +
3556: +#### duration
3557: +
3558: +The local `--duration` flag stops the capture after the given time (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). The default `0` captures until the command is interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Captures may run longer than an hour; see [Long captures](#long-captures).
3559: +
3560: +#### packet-limit
3561: +
3562: +The local `--packet-limit` flag stops the capture after that many packets, counted across all targets. `0`, the default, means no limit.
3563: +
3564: +#### snap-length
3565: +
3566: +The local `--snap-length` flag sets how many bytes of each packet are kept, from 64 to 1048576. The default `0` keeps 256 KiB.
3567: +
3568: +#### write
3569: +
3570: +The local `--write | -w` flag names the output file. The default `-` writes to stdout.
3571: +
3572: +#### list
3573: +
3574: +The local `--list` flag lists the interfaces `capture` accepts, for every running node, with the node and interface at the other end of each link, instead of capturing. `--format | -f` selects `table` (default) or `json`.
3575: +
3576: +### Output
3577: +
3578: +The output is one pcapng section:
3579: +
3580: +- a Section Header Block with `shb_userappl` set to `containerlab`
3581: +- one Interface Description Block per target, in the order of the `--target` flags, written before any packet: link type Ethernet, the snap length, nanosecond timestamps, and the name `<node>:<interface>` (for example `srl1:e1-1`), with the node named as the topology spells it
3582: +- Enhanced Packet Blocks of all targets, in timestamp order: packets are held briefly (100 ms with Docker and Podman, 250 ms with c9s) and written ordered by timestamp, so packets of different interfaces come out in order even though each one is read on its own; a packet that arrives later than that is written as it comes
3583: +
3584: +The interface name shows in Wireshark's interface column (`frame.interface_name`), so a capture of several nodes can be filtered by node and interface.
3585: +
3586: +When the capture ends (duration, packet limit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), the command finishes the stream and exits with code 0; the file is a valid capture. Status messages go to stderr. 3587: +
3588: +`--list -f json` prints an array:
3589: +
3590: +```json
3591: +[
3592: +  {
3593: +    "node": "srl1",
3594: +    "interface": "e1-1",
3595: +    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
3596: +    "peer_node": "srl2",
3597: +    "peer_interface": "ethernet-1/1"
3598: +  }
3599: +]
3600: +```
3601: +
3602: +`alias` is present only when the topology used an alias for the interface. `peer_node` is `host` for a host endpoint and `mgmt-net` for a management network endpoint.
3603: +
3604: +### How Docker and Podman captures work
3605: +
3606: +For each target, containerlab enters the node's network namespace, opens a Linux packet socket (`AF_PACKET`) bound to the interface, and leaves the namespace again; the socket keeps capturing on that interface. This is what `tcpdump` does inside the node, without needing `tcpdump` in the node or on the host. All sockets are opened before the first byte is written, so a capture that cannot start (a node that does not run, a missing interface) fails without output.
3607: +
3608: +- Packets carry the kernel's receive timestamps, so packets of different nodes compare on one clock.
3609: +- 802.1Q tags, which the kernel keeps outside the frame, are put back in place, so VLAN traffic shows its tags as on the wire.
3610: +- Each socket is in promiscuous mode for as long as it is open; the interface returns to its previous state when the capture ends.
3611: +- An interface that goes down and up again keeps being captured. When an interface disappears, for example while its node restarts, containerlab waits for it and reattaches once the node is back (`containerlab restart --node`). The time it was gone is reported as a warning with its start and end time.
3612: +
3613: +The command needs root (to open packet sockets and enter network namespaces), as other lab commands do.
3614: +
3615: +### Long captures
3616: +
3617: +Docker and Podman captures have no length limit. With c9s, one `clabwire` capture lasts at most one hour. `capture` chains captures: it starts the next one shortly before the current one ends, lets both run for a few seconds, and switches between them in the middle of that overlap. The repeated section and interface headers of the follow-up are dropped, and packets seen by both captures near the switch are written once (they are matched by content, because each capture stamps packets when it reads them). Once the switch time has passed, the previous capture is stopped through its stdin instead of running to its end. If a follow-up capture does not start in time, the missing interval is reported as a warning with its start and end time; it is never skipped silently. The timestamp order holds across switches: while one node's capture switches, packets of other nodes stamped after the switch wait for it.
3618: +
3619: +### Examples
3620: +
3621: +#### Capture two nodes for 30 seconds into one file
3622: +
3623: +```bash
3624: +containerlab capture -t srl.clab.yml \
3625: +  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
3626: +```
3627: +
3628: +#### Watch a capture live in Wireshark
3629: +
3630: +```bash
3631: +containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 -w - | wireshark -k -i -
3632: +```
3633: +

+// summarizePCAPNG returns the interface names of a little-endian pcapng stream and its IPv4 ICMP
+// packets per interface ID.
+func summarizePCAPNG(t *testing.T, data []byte) ([]string, map[uint32]int) {
+	t.Helper()
+
+	var names []string
+	icmp := map[uint32]int{}
+	for len(data) >= 12 {
+		blockType := binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(data[0:4])
+		length := int(binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(data[4:8]))
+		if length < 12 || length > len(data) {
+			t.Fatalf("invalid block length %d", length)
+		}
+		body := data[8 : length-4]
+		switch blockType {
+		case 1: // Interface Description Block
+			options := body[8:]
+			for len(options) >= 4 {
+				code := binary.LittleEndian.Uint16(options[0:2])
+				size := int(binary.LittleEndian.Uint16(options[2:4]))
+				if code == 0 {
+					break
+				}
+				if code == 2 {
+					names = append(names, string(options[4:4+size]))
+				}
+				options = options[4+size+(4-size%4)%4:]
+			}
+		case 6: // Enhanced Packet Block
+			id := binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(body[0:4])
+			frame := body[20 : 20+binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(body[12:16])]
+			if len(frame) > 23 && frame[12] == 0x08 && frame[13] == 0x00 && frame[23] == 1 {
+				icmp[id]++
+			}
+		}
+		data = data[length:]
+	}
+
+	return names, icmp
+}

+# capture command
+
+### Description
+
+The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.
+
+It works with every runtime:
+
+- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
+- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).
+
+The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.
+
+--8<-- "docs/cmd/deploy.md:env-vars-flags"
+
+### Usage
+
+`containerlab [global-flags] capture [local-flags]`
+
+### Flags
+
+#### topology | name
+
+Use the global `--topo | -t` flag to reference the lab topology file, or use the global `--name` flag to reference an already deployed lab by name. Without either, containerlab looks for a `*.clab.yml` file in the current directory, like the other lab commands.
+
+With Docker and Podman, the capturable interfaces are the links of the topology file, so `--name` needs the topology file the lab was deployed from to still be in place.
+
+#### target
+
+The local `--target` flag selects what to capture, as `<node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]`. Repeat it for more nodes:
+
+```text
+--target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 --target srl2:e1-1
+```
+
+The node name ends at the first colon, so interface names such as `1/1/3` or `ethernet-1/1` need no quoting. Node names are accepted as the topology file spells them; with Docker and Podman also as the container name (`clab-srl-srl1`), with c9s also as they were sanitized for Kubernetes (`R1` or `r1`). Interfaces are accepted by their name in the node or by the alias the topology used for them (`e1-1` or `ethernet-1/1` for SR Linux). `--list` shows both.
+
+Only lab link interfaces can be captured; the management interface cannot. An interface that is not a link interface of the node fails the command before anything is captured, and the error lists the node's capturable interfaces.
+
+#### duration
+
+The local `--duration` flag stops the capture after the given time (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). The default `0` captures until the command is interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Captures may run longer than an hour; see [Long captures](#long-captures).
+
+#### packet-limit
+
+The local `--packet-limit` flag stops the capture after that many packets, counted across all targets. `0`, the default, means no limit.
+
+#### snap-length
+
+The local `--snap-length` flag sets how many bytes of each packet are kept, from 64 to 1048576. The default `0` keeps 256 KiB.
+
+#### write
+
+The local `--write | -w` flag names the output file. The default `-` writes to stdout.
+
+#### list
+
+The local `--list` flag lists the interfaces `capture` accepts, for every running node, with the node and interface at the other end of each link, instead of capturing. `--format | -f` selects `table` (default) or `json`.
+
+### Output
+
+The output is one pcapng section:
+
+- a Section Header Block with `shb_userappl` set to `containerlab`
+- one Interface Description Block per target, in the order of the `--target` flags, written before any packet: link type Ethernet, the snap length, nanosecond timestamps, and the name `<node>:<interface>` (for example `srl1:e1-1`), with the node named as the topology spells it
+- Enhanced Packet Blocks of all targets, in timestamp order: packets are held briefly (100 ms with Docker and Podman, 250 ms with c9s) and written ordered by timestamp, so packets of different interfaces come out in order even though each one is read on its own; a packet that arrives later than that is written as it comes
+
+The interface name shows in Wireshark's interface column (`frame.interface_name`), so a capture of several nodes can be filtered by node and interface.
+
+When the capture ends (duration, packet limit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), the command finishes the stream and exits with code 0; the file is a valid capture. Status messages go to stderr. With c9s, every `clabwire` capture in the pods ends with the command: containerlab closes its stdin, and `clabwire` (`--stop-on-stdin-close`) stops.
+
+`--list -f json` prints an array:
+
+```json
+[
+  {
+    "node": "srl1",
+    "interface": "e1-1",
+    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
+    "peer_node": "srl2",
+    "peer_interface": "ethernet-1/1"
+  }
+]
+```
+
+`alias` is present only when the topology used an alias for the interface. `peer_node` is `host` for a host endpoint and `mgmt-net` for a management network endpoint.
+
+### How Docker and Podman captures work
+
+For each target, containerlab enters the node's network namespace, opens a Linux packet socket (`AF_PACKET`) bound to the interface, and leaves the namespace again; the socket keeps capturing on that interface. This is what `tcpdump` does inside the node, without needing `tcpdump` in the node or on the host. All sockets are opened before the first byte is written, so a capture that cannot start (a node that does not run, a missing interface) fails without output.
+
+- Packets carry the kernel's receive timestamps, so packets of different nodes compare on one clock.
+- 802.1Q tags, which the kernel keeps outside the frame, are put back in place, so VLAN traffic shows its tags as on the wire.
+- Each socket is in promiscuous mode for as long as it is open; the interface returns to its previous state when the capture ends.
+- An interface that goes down and up again keeps being captured. When an interface disappears, for example while its node restarts, containerlab waits for it and reattaches once the node is back (`containerlab restart --node`). The time it was gone is reported as a warning with its start and end time.
+
+The command needs root (to open packet sockets and enter network namespaces), as other lab commands do.
+
+### Long captures
+
+Docker and Podman captures have no length limit. With c9s, one `clabwire` capture lasts at most one hour. `capture` chains captures: it starts the next one shortly before the current one ends, lets both run for a few seconds, and switches between them in the middle of that overlap. The repeated section and interface headers of the follow-up are dropped, and packets seen by both captures near the switch are written once (they are matched by content, because each capture stamps packets when it reads them). Once the switch time has passed, the previous capture is stopped through its stdin instead of running to its end. If a follow-up capture does not start in time, the missing interval is reported as a warning with its start and end time; it is never skipped silently. The timestamp order holds across switches: while one node's capture switches, packets of other nodes stamped after the switch wait for it.
+
+### Examples
+
+#### Capture two nodes for 30 seconds into one file
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture -t srl.clab.yml \
+  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
+```
+
+#### Watch a capture live in Wireshark
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 -w - | wireshark -k -i -
+```
+
+#### Capture the first 100 packets with tshark
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:ethernet-1/1 --packet-limit 100 -w - | tshark -r -
+```
+
+#### List the capturable interfaces
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --list
+```
+
+#### Capture a c9s lab
+
+```bash
+containerlab -r c9s capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 -w srl.pcapng
+```

+## Packet capture
+
+[`containerlab capture`](../../cmd/capture.md) captures lab link interfaces of
+one or more nodes into one pcapng stream. Each node's pod runs the `clabwire`
+sidecar, which realized the node's links; containerlab execs its capture
+command (`/clabernetes/manager node-runtime packet-capture`) in the sidecar.
+No capture service runs in the cluster, and nothing is captured outside the
+lab's planned link interfaces.
+
+```bash
+# both ends of a link, for 30 seconds
+containerlab -r c9s capture -t clos.clab.yml \
+  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
+
+# live in Wireshark until Wireshark or Ctrl+C ends it
+containerlab -r c9s capture --name clos --target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 -w - | wireshark -k -i -

+containerlab -r c9s capture --name clos --list

+  per node, with `--nodeName`, every requested interface of that node,
+  `--format pcapng` and `--stop-on-stdin-close`, with stdin attached.
+- The streams are merged into one section: one Interface Description Block per
+  target named `<node>:<interface>` (the node as the topology spells it),
+  written before the first packet, and the packets of every target with their
+  interface IDs remapped.
+- Packets are written in timestamp order. Each node's stream arrives over its
+  own exec stream, so the merged stream holds every packet for 250 ms and
+  writes the held packets ordered by timestamp. A packet that arrives later
+  than that, stamped before a packet already written, is written as it comes;
+  the number of such packets goes to the debug log.

+  without `--duration`, chain captures with a few seconds of overlap and switch
+  in the middle of it; packets near the switch are matched by content so each
+  is written once. A follow-up that does not start in time is reported as a
+  gap, with its time span.

+  `c9s.direct-packet-capture-audit/v1alpha1`) with status `Denied` or `Failed`

+package clabernetes
+
+import (
+	"bytes"
+	"context"
+	"encoding/json"
+	"errors"
+	"fmt"
+	"hash/fnv"
+	"io"
+	"os"
+	"sort"
+	"strconv"
+	"strings"
+	"sync"
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/charmbracelet/log"
+	clabcapture "github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/capture"
+	clablabruntime "github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/labruntime"
+	"golang.org/x/sync/errgroup"
+)
+
+// The clabwire packet capture contract (clabernetes 0.11 or newer).
+const (
+	clabwireContainer = "clabwire"
+	clabwireManager   = "/clabernetes/manager"
+	// captureAuditSchema is the schema of the JSON audit lines clabwire writes to stderr.
+	captureAuditSchema = "c9s.direct-packet-capture-audit/v1alpha1"
+
+	captureAuditStarted   = "Started"
+	captureAuditSucceeded = "Succeeded"
+	captureAuditFailed    = "Failed"
+	captureAuditDenied    = "Denied"
+
+	// maxCaptureSegment is the longest single clabwire capture; longer captures are chained.
+	maxCaptureSegment = time.Hour
+	// maxClabwirePackets is the packet limit of a single clabwire capture.
+	maxClabwirePackets = 1_000_000
+	// maxCaptureOverlap is how long two chained segments run side by side.
+	maxCaptureOverlap = 10 * time.Second
+	// maxCaptureCutWindow is the half-width of the window around the cut in which packets of
+	// two segments are matched by content; it covers the difference between the timestamps
+	// two clabwire processes give the same packet.
+	maxCaptureCutWindow = 500 * time.Millisecond
+	// minCaptureSegment is the shortest segment the chain requests.
+	minCaptureSegment = 100 * time.Millisecond
+	// captureEndGrace is how long a capture with a duration waits for its last clabwire
+	// process to end after the duration passed.
+	captureEndGrace = 30 * time.Second
+	// captureStartRetries bounds the attempts to start a follow-up segment.
+	captureStartRetries = 3
+	// captureStdinCloseGrace is how long a segment's exec may take to end after its stdin was
+	// closed before the stream is cut.
+	captureStdinCloseGrace = 3 * time.Second
+	// clabwireStopOnStdinClose makes clabwire end a capture when its stdin closes. A
+	// Kubernetes exec does not stop its process when the stream ends, but it closes the
+	// process's stdin, so every capture runs with stdin attached and this flag.
+	clabwireStopOnStdinClose = "--stop-on-stdin-close"
+
+	// envCaptureSegment overrides the segment length. It exists to exercise chaining in tests
+	// without hour-long captures.
+	envCaptureSegment = "CLAB_C9S_CAPTURE_SEGMENT"
+	// defaultCaptureReorderWindow is how long the merged stream holds a packet back so packets
+	// of other nodes stamped earlier but delivered later still go out before it.
+	defaultCaptureReorderWindow = 250 * time.Millisecond
+	// envCaptureReorderWindow overrides the reorder window; 0 writes packets as they arrive.
+	// It is an internal knob, not a supported setting.
+	envCaptureReorderWindow = "CLAB_C9S_CAPTURE_REORDER_WINDOW"
+)

4491: +// captureChain runs the chained clabwire captures of one group.
4492: +//
4493: +// Chaining and the cut: segment k+1 starts `overlap` before segment k is due to end, so both
4494: +// capture the same packets for a while. clabwire stamps packets when it reads them, so two
4495: +// processes give the same packet timestamps a few microseconds apart, and timestamps alone
4496: +// cannot pair them. The chain therefore cuts in the middle of the overlap and matches packets by
4497: +// content close to the cut:
4498: +//
4499: +//  1. When segment k+1 reports Started (pod clock, from its audit record), the cut is
4500: +//     T = midpoint of [Started(k+1), Started(k) + duration(k)]: both segments run then.
4501: +//  2. Segment k keeps streaming live, but only packets stamped before T; it remembers the
4502: +//     content of what it wrote since segment k+1 started.
4503: +//  3. Segment k+1's packets are held back until segment k has ended. Then the ones stamped
4504: +//     before T-W are dropped (segment k had them), the ones stamped within W of T are dropped
4505: +//     when segment k wrote the same bytes on the same interface, and every other one is written.
4506: +//     From then on segment k+1 streams live.
4507: +//
4508: +// Once the pod clock passed T+W, segment k's stdin is closed so it ends without running to its
4509: +// planned end. While packets are held back, the chain holds the reorder buffer at T-W, so other
4510: +// nodes' later packets do not overtake them in the merged stream.
4511: +//
4512: +// W (500 ms, less for short test segments) covers the stamping difference. Identical frames on
4513: +// the same interface within W of the cut can be paired with each other, which can drop a true
4514: +// repeat; nothing else is lost or doubled. A follow-up segment that does not start in time leaves
4515: +// a gap, which is reported through CaptureRequest.OnGap (or logged), never silently ignored.

4518: +	group   *captureGroup

5591: +			f.written[node]++

5638: +// parsedCapture is a pcapng stream read back.
5639: +type parsedCapture struct {
5640: +	sections   int
5641: +	interfaces []string
5642: +	packets    []clabcapture.Packet
5643: +}
5644: +
5645: +func parseCapture(t *testing.T, data []byte) parsedCapture {
5646: +	t.Helper()
5647: +
5648: +	reader := clabcapture.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(data))
5649: +	var parsed parsedCapture
5650: +	for {
5651: +		event, err := reader.Next()
5652: +		if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
5653: +			break
5654: +		}
5655: +		if err != nil {
5656: +			t.Fatalf("invalid capture: %v", err)
5657: +		}
5658: +		if event.Interface != nil {
5659: +			if len(parsed.packets) != 0 {
5660: +				t.Fatal("interface description after the first packet")
5661: +			}
5662: +			if event.Interface.TSResol != 9 /* nanoseconds */ {
5663: +				t.Fatalf("interface %s tsresol = %d", event.Interface.Name, event.Interface.TSResol)
5664: +			}
5665: +			parsed.interfaces = append(parsed.interfaces, event.Interface.Name)
5666: +		}
5667: +		if event.Packet != nil {
5668: +			parsed.packets = append(parsed.packets, *event.Packet)
5669: +		}
5670: +	}
5671: +	parsed.sections = reader.Sections()
5672: +
5673: +	return parsed
5674: +}
5675: +
5676: +func packetSequence(packet clabcapture.Packet) uint64 {
5677: +	return binary.BigEndian.Uint64(packet.Data[0:8])
5678: +}
5679: +
5680: +func packetOrigin(packet clabcapture.Packet) string {
5681: +	return strings.TrimRight(string(packet.Data[8:]), "\x00")
5682: +}

5791: +

5801: +		OnGap:    func(gap clablabruntime.CaptureGap) { gaps = append(gaps, gap) },
5802: +	}, &out)
5803: +	if err != nil {
5804: +		t.Fatal(err)
5805: +	}
5806: +	if len(gaps) != 0 {
5807: +		t.Fatalf("gaps = %+v", gaps)
5808: +	}
5809: +	if processes := len(clabwire.captureCommands()); processes < 4 {
5810: +		t.Fatalf("capture processes = %d, want a chain of at least 4 segments", processes)
5811: +	}

5813: +	parsed := parseCapture(t, out.Bytes())

5817: +	}
5818: +	for id := range uint32(2) {
5819: +		var sequence []uint64
5820: +		for _, packet := range parsed.packets {

5827: +		}
5828: +		slices.Sort(sequence)
5829: +		for idx := 1; idx < len(sequence); idx++ {

5832: +				t.Fatalf("interface %d: tick %d written twice", id, sequence[idx])
5833: +			case sequence[idx] != sequence[idx-1]+1:
5834: +				t.Fatalf(

5836: +					id,
5837: +					sequence[idx-1]+1,
5838: +					sequence[idx]-1,
5839: +				)
5840: +			}
5841: +		}
5842: +	}
5843: +}

+// gatedWriter collects writes; once blocked, writes wait until open is closed.
+type gatedWriter struct {
+	open chan struct{}
+
+	mu      sync.Mutex
+	blocked bool
+	data    bytes.Buffer
+}
+
+func (w *gatedWriter) block() {
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	w.blocked = true
+	w.mu.Unlock()
+}
+
+func (w *gatedWriter) Write(data []byte) (int, error) {
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	blocked := w.blocked
+	w.mu.Unlock()
+	if blocked {
+		<-w.open
+	}
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	defer w.mu.Unlock()
+
+	return w.data.Write(data)
+}
+
+func (w *gatedWriter) bytes() []byte {
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	defer w.mu.Unlock()
+
+	return w.data.Bytes()
+}

+func TestCaptureClosesStdinWhenItEnds(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	targets := []clablabruntime.CaptureTarget{
+		{Node: "r1", Interface: "e1-1"},
+		{Node: "r2", Interface: "e1-1"},
+	}
+
+	t.Run("cancel", func(t *testing.T) {
+		t.Parallel()
+
+		r, clabwire := captureTestRuntime(t, 2*time.Millisecond)
+		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 200*time.Millisecond)
+		defer cancel()
+
+		if err := r.Capture(ctx, clablabruntime.CaptureRequest{Name: "lab1", Targets: targets},
+			io.Discard); err != nil {
+			t.Fatal(err)
+		}
+		requireStdinClosedEverywhere(t, clabwire)
+	})
+
+	t.Run("output fails", func(t *testing.T) {
+		t.Parallel()
+
+		r, clabwire := captureTestRuntime(t, 2*time.Millisecond)
+		output := &failingWriter{accept: 3}
+		err := r.Capture(context.Background(), clablabruntime.CaptureRequest{
+			Name: "lab1", Targets: targets, Duration: time.Hour,
+		}, output)
+		if err == nil || !strings.Contains(err.Error(), "broken pipe") {
+			t.Fatalf("Capture() = %v, want the write error", err)
+		}
+		requireStdinClosedEverywhere(t, clabwire)
+	})
+}
+
+// failingWriter accepts some writes, then fails like a closed pipe.
+type failingWriter struct {
+	mu     sync.Mutex
+	accept int
+}
+
+func (w *failingWriter) Write(data []byte) (int, error) {
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	defer w.mu.Unlock()
+	if w.accept == 0 {
+		return 0, errors.New("write |1: broken pipe")
+	}
+	w.accept--
+
+	return len(data), nil
+}
+
+func requireStdinClosedEverywhere(t *testing.T, clabwire *fakeClabwire) {
+	t.Helper()
+
+	clabwire.mu.Lock()
+	defer clabwire.mu.Unlock()
+	for _, node := range []string{"r1", "r2"} {
+		if clabwire.processes[node] == 0 || clabwire.stdinClosed[node] != clabwire.processes[node] {
+			t.Fatalf("%s: %d processes, %d ended through stdin", node,
+				clabwire.processes[node], clabwire.stdinClosed[node])
+		}
+	}
+}
+
+// TestCaptureRejectsAClabwireWithoutStopOnStdinClose turns the usage error of an older clabwire
+// into the release error.
+func TestCaptureRejectsAClabwireWithoutStopOnStdinClose(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	r, clabwire := captureTestRuntime(t, time.Millisecond)
+	clabwire.stderrOnly = "flag provided but not defined: -stop-on-stdin-close"
+
+	err := r.Capture(context.Background(), clablabruntime.CaptureRequest{
+		Name: "lab1", Targets: []clablabruntime.CaptureTarget{{Node: "r2", Interface: "e1-1"}},
+		Duration: time.Second,

+	if !errors.Is(err, clablabruntime.ErrUnsupportedRuntimeVersion) ||

+		!strings.Contains(err.Error(), "(0.11 or newer)") {
+		t.Fatalf("Capture() = %v, want the release error", err)
+	}
+}
+
+// requireTimeOrdered checks that the merged stream's timestamps never decrease.
+func requireTimeOrdered(t *testing.T, packets []clabcapture.Packet) {
+	t.Helper()
+
+	for idx := 1; idx < len(packets); idx++ {
+		if packets[idx].Timestamp < packets[idx-1].Timestamp {
+			t.Fatalf("packet %d (%s) at %d precedes packet %d (%s) at %d", idx,
+				packetOrigin(packets[idx]), packets[idx].Timestamp, idx-1,
+				packetOrigin(packets[idx-1]), packets[idx-1].Timestamp)
+		}
+	}
+}

+// TestCaptureMergesNodesInTimestampOrder merges two nodes whose streams arrive with different
+// delays: r2's packets are stamped 60 ms before they reach containerlab. The reorder window puts
+// them in order; without it they are not.
+func TestCaptureMergesNodesInTimestampOrder(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	for _, reorder := range []bool{true, false} {
+		t.Run(fmt.Sprintf("reorder=%v", reorder), func(t *testing.T) {
+			t.Parallel()
+
+			r, clabwire := captureTestRuntime(t, 5*time.Millisecond)
+			clabwire.stampSkew["r2"] = 60 * time.Millisecond
+			if !reorder {
+				r.captureReorderWindow = -1
+			}
+
+			var out bytes.Buffer
+			err := r.Capture(context.Background(), clablabruntime.CaptureRequest{
+				Name: "lab1",
+				Targets: []clablabruntime.CaptureTarget{
+					{Node: "r1", Interface: "e1-1"},
+					{Node: "r2", Interface: "e1-1"},
+				},
+				Duration: 500 * time.Millisecond,
+			}, &out)
+			if err != nil {
+				t.Fatal(err)
+			}
+
+			packets := parseCapture(t, out.Bytes()).packets
+			ordered := slices.IsSortedFunc(packets, func(a, b clabcapture.Packet) int {
+				return int(a.Timestamp - b.Timestamp)
+			})
+			if reorder {
+				requireTimeOrdered(t, packets)
+			} else if ordered {
+				t.Fatal("the skewed streams came out ordered without the reorder window")
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}
+
+// TestCaptureChainsSeveralNodesInOrderWithoutDuplicates chains two nodes with skewed streams and a
+// reorder window shorter than a segment switch:
+// every tick appears exactly once per interface and the merged stream stays in timestamp order
+// across every segment switch, while old segments are ended through stdin at the switch.
+func TestCaptureChainsSeveralNodesInOrderWithoutDuplicates(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	r, clabwire := captureTestRuntime(t, 4*time.Millisecond)
+	r.captureSegment = 300 * time.Millisecond
+	// a window shorter than a switch: the chains' holds keep the order across the switches
+	r.captureReorderWindow = 15 * time.Millisecond
+	clabwire.stampSkew["r2"] = 5 * time.Millisecond
+	// r2 switches segments 120 ms after r1, so one chain streams live while the other holds
+	clabwire.firstStartDelay["r2"] = 120 * time.Millisecond
+
+	var gaps []clablabruntime.CaptureGap
+	var out bytes.Buffer
+	err := r.Capture(context.Background(), clablabruntime.CaptureRequest{
+		Name: "lab1",
+		Targets: []clablabruntime.CaptureTarget{
+			{Node: "r1", Interface: "e1-1"},
+			{Node: "r2", Interface: "e1-1"},
+		},
+		Duration: 1300 * time.Millisecond,
+		OnGap:    func(gap clablabruntime.CaptureGap) { gaps = append(gaps, gap) },
+	}, &out)
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	if len(gaps) != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("gaps = %+v", gaps)
+	}

+	for id := range uint32(2) {
+		var sequence []uint64
+		for _, packet := range parsed.packets {
+			if packet.InterfaceID == id {
+				sequence = append(sequence, packetSequence(packet))
+			}
+		}
+		slices.Sort(sequence)
+		if len(sequence) < 200 {

+		}
+		for idx := 1; idx < len(sequence); idx++ {

+				t.Fatalf("interface %d: tick %d followed by %d", id, sequence[idx-1], sequence[idx])
+			}
+		}
+	}
+
+	clabwire.mu.Lock()
+	defer clabwire.mu.Unlock()
+	for _, node := range []string{"r1", "r2"} {
+		if clabwire.processes[node] < 4 || clabwire.stdinClosed[node] == 0 {
+			t.Fatalf("%s: %d processes, %d stopped through stdin at a switch", node,
+				clabwire.processes[node], clabwire.stdinClosed[node])
+		}
+	}
+}

+func TestCaptureReorderWindowKnob(t *testing.T) {

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+# Copyright 2020 Nokia
+# Licensed under the BSD 3-Clause License.
+# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
+"""Summarize a little-endian pcapng file as containerlab capture writes it, as JSON.
+
+Prints the number of sections, the interface names in order, the packet count per interface,
+whether packets are in timestamp order, the number of 802.1Q tagged frames and the number of
+ICMP echo requests and replies (untagged or tagged).
+"""
+
+import json
+import struct
+import sys
+
+SHB, IDB, EPB = 0x0A0D0D0A, 0x00000001, 0x00000006
+
+
+def main(path):
+    with open(path, "rb") as f:
+        data = f.read()
+
+    sections, names, counts, stamps = 0, [], {}, []
+    vlan, echo = 0, 0
+    offset = 0
+    while offset < len(data):
+        block_type, length = struct.unpack_from("<II", data, offset)
+        body = data[offset + 8 : offset + length - 4]
+        if block_type == SHB:
+            sections += 1
+        elif block_type == IDB:
+            options, name = body[8:], ""
+            while len(options) >= 4:
+                code, size = struct.unpack_from("<HH", options)
+                if code == 0:
+                    break
+                if code == 2:
+                    name = options[4 : 4 + size].decode()
+                options = options[4 + size + (4 - size % 4) % 4 :]
+            names.append(name)
+        elif block_type == EPB:
+            iface, high, low, captured = struct.unpack_from("<IIII", body)
+            frame = body[20 : 20 + captured]
+            counts[names[iface]] = counts.get(names[iface], 0) + 1
+            stamps.append(high << 32 | low)
+            ethertype, l3 = struct.unpack_from(">H", frame, 12)[0], 14
+            if ethertype == 0x8100:
+                vlan += 1
+                ethertype, l3 = struct.unpack_from(">H", frame, 16)[0], 18
+            if ethertype == 0x0800 and frame[l3 + 9] == 1 and frame[l3 + 20] in (0, 8):
+                echo += 1
+        offset += length
+
+    print(
+        json.dumps(
+            {
+                "sections": sections,
+                "interfaces": names,
+                "packets": counts,
+                "ordered": stamps == sorted(stamps),
+                "vlan_frames": vlan,
+                "icmp_echo": echo,
+            }
+        )
+    )
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    main(sys.argv[1])

+#!/bin/sh
+# Prints the packet-capture processes running in the clabwire container of a c9s node's pod.
+# usage: clabwire-captures.sh <namespace> <node>
+#
+# A process of a Kubernetes exec is not visible through the API, so this looks at the worker
+# that runs the pod: a KinD node, which is a Docker container. It lists the processes whose
+# cgroup belongs to the clabwire container. Exits 2 when the worker is not a Docker container.
+set -eu
+
+namespace=$1
+node=$2
+
+pod=$(kubectl -n "$namespace" get pod -l "c9s.run/topologyNode=$node" \
+  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
+worker=$(kubectl -n "$namespace" get pod "$pod" -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')
+# clabwire is a sidecar (an init container that keeps running)
+container=$(kubectl -n "$namespace" get pod "$pod" -o jsonpath=\
+'{.status.initContainerStatuses[?(@.name=="clabwire")].containerID}{.status.containerStatuses[?(@.name=="clabwire")].containerID}')
+container=${container#*://}
+
+if ! docker inspect --type container "$worker" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+  echo "worker $worker of pod $namespace/$pod is not a Docker container (KinD)" >&2
+  exit 2
+fi
+if [ -z "$container" ]; then
+  echo "pod $namespace/$pod has no running clabwire container" >&2
+  exit 1
+fi
+
+docker exec "$worker" sh -c "
+  for proc in /proc/[0-9]*; do
+    if grep -qs '$container' \"\$proc/cgroup\"; then
+      tr '\\0' ' ' < \"\$proc/cmdline\" 2>/dev/null && echo
+    fi
+  done" | grep 'packet-capture' || true

3517: +# capture command
3518: +
3519: +### Description
3520: +
3521: +The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.
3522: +
3523: +It works with every runtime:
3524: +
3525: +- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
3526: +- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).
3527: +
3528: +The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.
3529: +
3530: +--8<-- "docs/cmd/deploy.md:env-vars-flags"
3531: +
3532: +### Usage
3533: +
3534: +`containerlab [global-flags] capture [local-flags]`
3535: +
3536: +### Flags
3537: +
3538: +#### topology | name
3539: +
3540: +Use the global `--topo | -t` flag to reference the lab topology file, or use the global `--name` flag to reference an already deployed lab by name. Without either, containerlab looks for a `*.clab.yml` file in the current directory, like the other lab commands.
3541: +
3542: +With Docker and Podman, the capturable interfaces are the links of the topology file, so `--name` needs the topology file the lab was deployed from to still be in place.
3543: +
3544: +#### target
3545: +
3546: +The local `--target` flag selects what to capture, as `<node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]`. Repeat it for more nodes:
3547: +
3548: +```text
3549: +--target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 --target srl2:e1-1
3550: +```
3551: +
3552: +The node name ends at the first colon, so interface names such as `1/1/3` or `ethernet-1/1` need no quoting. Node names are accepted as the topology file spells them; with Docker and Podman also as the container name (`clab-srl-srl1`), with c9s also as they were sanitized for Kubernetes (`R1` or `r1`). Interfaces are accepted by their name in the node or by the alias the topology used for them (`e1-1` or `ethernet-1/1` for SR Linux). `--list` shows both.
3553: +
3554: +Only lab link interfaces can be captured; the management interface cannot. An interface that is not a link interface of the node fails the command before anything is captured, and the error lists the node's capturable interfaces.
3555: +
3556: +#### duration
3557: +
3558: +The local `--duration` flag stops the capture after the given time (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). The default `0` captures until the command is interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Captures may run longer than an hour; see [Long captures](#long-captures).
3559: +
3560: +#### packet-limit
3561: +
3562: +The local `--packet-limit` flag stops the capture after that many packets, counted across all targets. `0`, the default, means no limit.
3563: +
3564: +#### snap-length
3565: +
3566: +The local `--snap-length` flag sets how many bytes of each packet are kept, from 64 to 1048576. The default `0` keeps 256 KiB.
3567: +
3568: +#### write
3569: +
3570: +The local `--write | -w` flag names the output file. The default `-` writes to stdout.
3571: +
3572: +#### list
3573: +
3574: +The local `--list` flag lists the interfaces `capture` accepts, for every running node, with the node and interface at the other end of each link, instead of capturing. `--format | -f` selects `table` (default) or `json`.
3575: +
3576: +### Output
3577: +
3578: +The output is one pcapng section:
3579: +
3580: +- a Section Header Block with `shb_userappl` set to `containerlab`
3581: +- one Interface Description Block per target, in the order of the `--target` flags, written before any packet: link type Ethernet, the snap length, nanosecond timestamps, and the name `<node>:<interface>` (for example `srl1:e1-1`), with the node named as the topology spells it
3582: +- Enhanced Packet Blocks of all targets, in timestamp order: packets are held briefly (100 ms with Docker and Podman, 250 ms with c9s) and written ordered by timestamp, so packets of different interfaces come out in order even though each one is read on its own; a packet that arrives later than that is written as it comes
3583: +
3584: +The interface name shows in Wireshark's interface column (`frame.interface_name`), so a capture of several nodes can be filtered by node and interface.
3585: +
3586: +When the capture ends (duration, packet limit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), the command finishes the stream and exits with code 0; the file is a valid capture. Status messages go to stderr. With c9s, every `clabwire` capture in the pods ends with the command: containerlab closes its stdin, and `clabwire` (`--stop-on-stdin-close`) stops.
3587: +
3588: +`--list -f json` prints an array:
3589: +
3590: +```json
3591: +[
3592: +  {
3593: +    "node": "srl1",
3594: +    "interface": "e1-1",
3595: +    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
3596: +    "peer_node": "srl2",
3597: +    "peer_interface": "ethernet-1/1"
3598: +  }
3599: +]
3600: +```
3601: +
3602: +`alias` is present only when the topology used an alias for the interface. `peer_node` is `host` for a host endpoint and `mgmt-net` for a management network endpoint.
3603: +
3604: +### How Docker and Podman captures work
3605: +
3606: +For each target, containerlab enters the node's network namespace, opens a Linux packet socket (`AF_PACKET`) bound to the interface, and leaves the namespace again; the socket keeps capturing on that interface. This is what `tcpdump` does inside the node, without needing `tcpdump` in the node or on the host. All sockets are opened before the first byte is written, so a capture that cannot start (a node that does not run, a missing interface) fails without output.
3607: +
3608: +- Packets carry the kernel's receive timestamps, so packets of different nodes compare on one clock.
3609: +- 802.1Q tags, which the kernel keeps outside the frame, are put back in place, so VLAN traffic shows its tags as on the wire.
3610: +- Each socket is in promiscuous mode for as long as it is open; the interface returns to its previous state when the capture ends.
3611: +- An interface that goes down and up again keeps being captured. When an interface disappears, for example while its node restarts, containerlab waits for it and reattaches once the node is back (`containerlab restart --node`). The time it was gone is reported as a warning with its start and end time.
3612: +
3613: +The command needs root (to open packet sockets and enter network namespaces), as other lab commands do.
3614: +
3615: +### Long captures
3616: +
3617: +Docker and Podman captures have no length limit. With c9s, one `clabwire` capture lasts at most one hour. `capture` chains captures: it starts the next one shortly before the current one ends, lets both run for a few seconds, and switches between them in the middle of that overlap. The repeated section and interface headers of the follow-up are dropped, and packets seen by both captures near the switch are written once (they are matched by content, because each capture stamps packets when it reads them). Once the switch time has passed, the previous capture is stopped through its stdin instead of running to its end. If a follow-up capture does not start in time, the missing interval is reported as a warning with its start and end time; it is never skipped silently. The timestamp order holds across switches: while one node's capture switches, packets of other nodes stamped after the switch wait for it.
3618: +
3619: +### Examples
3620: +
3621: +#### Capture two nodes for 30 seconds into one file
3622: +
3623: +```bash
3624: +containerlab capture -t srl.clab.yml \
3625: +  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
3626: +```
3627: +
3628: +#### Watch a capture live in Wireshark
3629: +
3630: +```bash
3631: +containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 -w - | wireshark -k -i -
3632: +```
3633: +
3634: +#### Capture the first 100 packets with tshark
3635: +
3636: +```bash
3637: +containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:ethernet-1/1 --packet-limit 100 -w - | tshark -r -
3638: +```
3639: +
3640: +#### List the capturable interfaces
3641: +
3642: +```bash
3643: +containerlab capture --name srl --list
3644: +```
3645: +
3646: +#### Capture a c9s lab
3647: +
3648: +```bash
3649: +containerlab -r c9s capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 -w srl.pcapng
3650: +```

@@ -0,0 +1,134 @@
+# capture command
+
+### Description
+
+The `capture` command captures packets on lab link interfaces of one or more nodes and writes them as one [pcapng](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-03.html) stream, to a file or to stdout for Wireshark.
+
+It works with every runtime:
+
+- **Docker and Podman**: containerlab opens a packet socket on each interface inside the node's network namespace. Nothing runs in the node, the node image needs no capture tools, and no extra software is needed on the host: the command needs root, like `deploy`. See [How Docker and Podman captures work](#how-docker-and-podman-captures-work).
+- **c9s**: the `clabwire` sidecar of each node's pod captures the packets; see the [c9s runtime](../manual/clabernetes/runtime.md#packet-capture).
+
+The output is the same with both. [Edgeshark](../manual/wireshark.md) remains an alternative for Docker labs when you prefer to pick interfaces in a GUI.
+
+--8<-- "docs/cmd/deploy.md:env-vars-flags"
+
+### Usage
+
+`containerlab [global-flags] capture [local-flags]`
+
+### Flags
+
+#### topology | name
+
+Use the global `--topo | -t` flag to reference the lab topology file, or use the global `--name` flag to reference an already deployed lab by name. Without either, containerlab looks for a `*.clab.yml` file in the current directory, like the other lab commands.
+
+With Docker and Podman, the capturable interfaces are the links of the topology file, so `--name` needs the topology file the lab was deployed from to still be in place.
+
+#### target
+
+The local `--target` flag selects what to capture, as `<node>:<interface>[,<interface>...]`. Repeat it for more nodes:
+
+```text
+--target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 --target srl2:e1-1
+```
+
+The node name ends at the first colon, so interface names such as `1/1/3` or `ethernet-1/1` need no quoting. Node names are accepted as the topology file spells them; with Docker and Podman also as the container name (`clab-srl-srl1`), with c9s also as they were sanitized for Kubernetes (`R1` or `r1`). Interfaces are accepted by their name in the node or by the alias the topology used for them (`e1-1` or `ethernet-1/1` for SR Linux). `--list` shows both.
+
+Only lab link interfaces can be captured; the management interface cannot. An interface that is not a link interface of the node fails the command before anything is captured, and the error lists the node's capturable interfaces.
+
+#### duration
+
+The local `--duration` flag stops the capture after the given time (`30s`, `5m`, `2h`). The default `0` captures until the command is interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Captures may run longer than an hour; see [Long captures](#long-captures).
+
+#### packet-limit
+
+The local `--packet-limit` flag stops the capture after that many packets, counted across all targets. `0`, the default, means no limit.
+
+#### snap-length
+
+The local `--snap-length` flag sets how many bytes of each packet are kept, from 64 to 1048576. The default `0` keeps 256 KiB.
+
+#### write
+
+The local `--write | -w` flag names the output file. The default `-` writes to stdout.
+
+#### list
+
+The local `--list` flag lists the interfaces `capture` accepts, for every running node, with the node and interface at the other end of each link, instead of capturing. `--format | -f` selects `table` (default) or `json`.
+
+### Output
+
+The output is one pcapng section:
+
+- a Section Header Block with `shb_userappl` set to `containerlab`
+- one Interface Description Block per target, in the order of the `--target` flags, written before any packet: link type Ethernet, the snap length, nanosecond timestamps, and the name `<node>:<interface>` (for example `srl1:e1-1`), with the node named as the topology spells it
+- Enhanced Packet Blocks of all targets, in timestamp order: packets are held briefly (100 ms with Docker and Podman, 250 ms with c9s) and written ordered by timestamp, so packets of different interfaces come out in order even though each one is read on its own; a packet that arrives later than that is written as it comes
+
+The interface name shows in Wireshark's interface column (`frame.interface_name`), so a capture of several nodes can be filtered by node and interface.
+
+When the capture ends (duration, packet limit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), the command finishes the stream and exits with code 0; the file is a valid capture. Status messages go to stderr. With c9s, every `clabwire` capture in the pods ends with the command: containerlab closes its stdin, and `clabwire` (`--stop-on-stdin-close`) stops.
+
+`--list -f json` prints an array:
+
+```json
+[
+  {
+    "node": "srl1",
+    "interface": "e1-1",
+    "alias": "ethernet-1/1",
+    "peer_node": "srl2",
+    "peer_interface": "ethernet-1/1"
+  }
+]
+```
+
+`alias` is present only when the topology used an alias for the interface. `peer_node` is `host` for a host endpoint and `mgmt-net` for a management network endpoint.
+
+### How Docker and Podman captures work
+
+For each target, containerlab enters the node's network namespace, opens a Linux packet socket (`AF_PACKET`) bound to the interface, and leaves the namespace again; the socket keeps capturing on that interface. This is what `tcpdump` does inside the node, without needing `tcpdump` in the node or on the host. All sockets are opened before the first byte is written, so a capture that cannot start (a node that does not run, a missing interface) fails without output.
+
+- Packets carry the kernel's receive timestamps, so packets of different nodes compare on one clock.
+- 802.1Q tags, which the kernel keeps outside the frame, are put back in place, so VLAN traffic shows its tags as on the wire.
+- Each socket is in promiscuous mode for as long as it is open; the interface returns to its previous state when the capture ends.
+- An interface that goes down and up again keeps being captured. When an interface disappears, for example while its node restarts, containerlab waits for it and reattaches once the node is back (`containerlab restart --node`). The time it was gone is reported as a warning with its start and end time.
+
+The command needs root (to open packet sockets and enter network namespaces), as other lab commands do.
+
+### Long captures
+
+Docker and Podman captures have no length limit. With c9s, one `clabwire` capture lasts at most one hour. `capture` chains captures: it starts the next one shortly before the current one ends, lets both run for a few seconds, and switches between them in the middle of that overlap. The repeated section and interface headers of the follow-up are dropped, and packets seen by both captures near the switch are written once (they are matched by content, because each capture stamps packets when it reads them). Once the switch time has passed, the previous capture is stopped through its stdin instead of running to its end. If a follow-up capture does not start in time, the missing interval is reported as a warning with its start and end time; it is never skipped silently. The timestamp order holds across switches: while one node's capture switches, packets of other nodes stamped after the switch wait for it.
+
+### Examples
+
+#### Capture two nodes for 30 seconds into one file
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture -t srl.clab.yml \
+  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
+```
+
+#### Watch a capture live in Wireshark
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1,e1-2 -w - | wireshark -k -i -
+```
+
+#### Capture the first 100 packets with tshark
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --target srl1:ethernet-1/1 --packet-limit 100 -w - | tshark -r -
+```
+
+#### List the capturable interfaces
+
+```bash
+containerlab capture --name srl --list
+```
+
+#### Capture a c9s lab
+
+```bash
+containerlab -r c9s capture --name srl --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 -w srl.pcapng
+```
